Special laws add others: RA 10175 Sec. 6 (one degree higher for ICT-committed crimes), RA 10591 Sec. 29 (use of a loose firearm), RA 9165 Sec. 25 (offender under the influence of drugs as qualifying aggravating).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14; Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175), Sec. 6

q: Omar, high on shabu (as shown by a positive drug test), attacked a victim from behind without warning, killing him with an unlicensed gun. What aggravating circumstances are present?

alac.answer: Treachery (which qualifies the killing to murder), the use of a loose firearm, and being under the influence of dangerous drugs are present.
alac.basis: Article 14(16) of the Revised Penal Code provides that there is treachery when the offender employs means which tend directly and specially to insure the execution of the crime, without risk to himself arising from the defense which the offended party might make. Section 29 of RA 10591 provides that the use of a loose firearm, when inherent in the commission of a crime, shall be considered an aggravating circumstance. Section 25 of RA 9165 provides that a positive finding for the use of dangerous drugs shall be a qualifying aggravating circumstance in the commission of a crime by an offender.
alac.application: Here, Omar attacked from behind without warning, so the victim could not defend himself: treachery, which qualifies the killing to murder. He used an unlicensed gun, a loose firearm. He tested positive for drugs.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Omar is liable for murder, with the aggravating circumstances of use of a loose firearm and being under the influence of dangerous drugs, which affect the penalty.

keyPoints: Treachery (Art. 14(16)) qualifies the killing to murder
Use of loose firearm is aggravating (RA 10591, Sec. 29)
Drug influence is a qualifying aggravating circumstance (RA 9165, Sec. 25)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14; RA 10591, Sec. 29; RA 9165, Sec. 25

q: Under Article 15 of the Revised Penal Code, the alternative circumstances are:
choices: Relationship, intoxication, and the degree of instruction and education of the offender
hints: They may aggravate or mitigate depending on the crime.
Intoxication mitigates if not habitual or intentional.
why: RPC Art. 15: alternative circumstances (relationship, intoxication, degree of instruction) are aggravating or mitigating depending on the nature and effects of the crime; intoxication mitigates if not habitual or subsequent to the plan, and aggravates if habitual or intentional.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 15

q: Pia, who is not a habitual drinker, got drunk at a party and, in a sudden quarrel, slapped and seriously injured her cousin. Separately, Quino drank heavily to gain courage before attacking his enemy as planned. How does intoxication affect their liability?

alac.answer: Intoxication mitigates Pia's liability but aggravates Quino's.
alac.basis: Article 15 of the Revised Penal Code provides that intoxication shall be taken into consideration as a mitigating circumstance when the offender has committed a felony in a state of intoxication, if the same is not habitual or subsequent to the plan to commit the felony; but when the intoxication is habitual or intentional, it shall be considered as an aggravating circumstance.
alac.application: Here, Pia is not a habitual drinker, and her intoxication was not planned to commit the crime; the quarrel was sudden. Quino deliberately drank to embolden himself to carry out a planned attack, so his intoxication was intentional.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pia's intoxication is mitigating, while Quino's is aggravating. (Relationship, as an alternative circumstance, may also be considered in Pia's case depending on the crime.)

keyPoints: Alternative circumstances (Art. 15)
Intoxication mitigates if not habitual or not planned
Habitual or intentional intoxication aggravates
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 15

q: Under Article 332 of the Revised Penal Code, which is an absolutory cause for theft, swindling or malicious mischief?
choices: The crime is committed mutually between spouses, ascendants and descendants, or brothers and sisters living together, among others
The offender is a public officer
hints: Absolutory causes: the act is criminal, but no penalty is imposed for policy reasons.
Civil liability remains.
why: Absolutory causes exempt from penalty despite the crime, e.g., Art. 20 (relatives as accessories), Art. 247 (death or injuries under exceptional circumstances: destierro only), Art. 332 (theft, swindling, malicious mischief between close relatives: civil liability only).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 20, 247 and 332

q: Rina took her mother's jewelry and sold it to pay her debts. Separately, Sam, a married man, surprised his wife in the act of sexual intercourse with another man and immediately killed the man. What are their liabilities?

alac.answer: Rina has no criminal liability but must answer civilly; Sam suffers only destierro.
alac.basis: Article 332 of the Revised Penal Code provides that no criminal, but only civil liability, shall result from the commission of the crime of theft, swindling or malicious mischief committed or caused mutually by spouses, ascendants and descendants, among others. Article 247 provides that any legally married person who, having surprised his spouse in the act of committing sexual intercourse with another person, shall kill any of them or both in the act or immediately thereafter, shall suffer the penalty of destierro.
alac.application: Here, Rina, a descendant, took her mother's jewelry, which is theft between a descendant and an ascendant, covered by Article 332. Sam, legally married, surprised his wife in the act of intercourse and immediately killed the man, which falls under Article 247.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rina is only civilly liable to her mother, and Sam is punished only by destierro.

keyPoints: Absolutory causes
Theft among close relatives: civil liability only (Art. 332)
Death under exceptional circumstances: destierro (Art. 247)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 247 and 332

q: Under Article 14(9) of the Revised Penal Code, a recidivist is one who, at the time of his trial for one crime:
choices: Has been previously convicted by final judgment of another crime embraced in the same title of the Code
hints: Both crimes must be in the same title of the RPC.
Pardon does not erase recidivism.
why: RPC Art. 14(9): recidivism requires a previous conviction by final judgment of another crime embraced in the same title of the Code, at the time of trial for the new crime; it is a generic aggravating circumstance.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14(9)

q: Tom was convicted by final judgment of theft in 2018. In 2024, he committed estafa and, during his trial, the 2018 conviction was proved. Is he a recidivist? What if his prior final conviction had been for homicide?

alac.answer: Yes, he is a recidivist, because theft and estafa are both crimes against property; if his prior conviction were for homicide, he would not be a recidivist.
alac.basis: Article 14(9) of the Revised Penal Code provides that a recidivist is one who, at the time of his trial for one crime, shall have been previously convicted by final judgment of another crime embraced in the same title of the Code.
alac.application: Here, theft and estafa both fall under Title Ten, Crimes Against Property, and Tom's prior conviction for theft was by final judgment before his trial for estafa. Homicide, by contrast, belongs to Title Eight, Crimes Against Persons, a different title.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, recidivism aggravates Tom's estafa; a prior homicide conviction would not make him a recidivist (though it might support reiteracion if the conditions are met).

keyPoints: Recidivism: prior final conviction (Art. 14(9))
Both crimes in the same title of the RPC
Generic aggravating circumstance
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14(9)

q: Under Article 160 of the Revised Penal Code, quasi-recidivism exists when a person:
choices: Commits two crimes on the same day
Commits a felony after having been convicted by final judgment, before beginning to serve sentence or while serving it
hints: It is a special aggravating circumstance.
The new felony gets the maximum period of its penalty.
why: RPC Art. 160: one who commits a felony after final conviction, before or while serving sentence, is punished with the maximum period of the penalty for the new felony; it cannot be offset by mitigating circumstances.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 160

q: Uly, serving a final sentence for drug trafficking, killed a fellow inmate. He pleaded guilty, claiming the mitigating circumstance to lower the penalty. How should his penalty be determined?

alac.answer: The penalty for the killing should be imposed in its maximum period because of quasi-recidivism, which cannot be offset by his plea of guilty.
alac.basis: Article 160 of the Revised Penal Code provides that any person who shall commit a felony after having been convicted by final judgment, before beginning to serve such sentence, or while serving the same, shall be punished by the maximum period of the penalty prescribed by law for the new felony. Quasi-recidivism is a special aggravating circumstance that cannot be offset by ordinary mitigating circumstances. The first crime need not be a felony, but the new one must be.
alac.application: Here, Uly was serving a final sentence for drug trafficking (a crime under a special law) when he committed a new felony, the killing of an inmate. Quasi-recidivism applies, so the maximum period of the penalty for the killing must be imposed, notwithstanding his plea of guilty.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Uly's penalty for the killing is the maximum period of the prescribed penalty.

keyPoints: Quasi-recidivism (Art. 160)
New felony after final conviction, while serving sentence
Maximum period; not offset by mitigating circumstances
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 160

q: Under Article 14(10) of the Revised Penal Code, reiteracion (habituality) exists when the offender has been previously punished for:
choices: An offense in the same title
An offense to which the law attaches an equal or greater penalty, or for two or more crimes to which it attaches a lighter penalty
hints: Previous punishment (service of sentence) is required.
Unlike recidivism, the crimes need not be in the same title.
why: RPC Art. 14(10): reiteracion requires that the offender has been previously punished for an offense with an equal or greater penalty, or for two or more offenses with lighter penalties; the crimes need not be in the same title.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14(10)

q: Vito served sentences for serious physical injuries (prision correccional) and for slander (arresto mayor). He is now on trial for theft punished by prision correccional. Is reiteracion present?

alac.answer: Yes, reiteracion is present.
alac.basis: Article 14(10) of the Revised Penal Code provides as an aggravating circumstance that the offender has been previously punished for an offense to which the law attaches an equal or greater penalty, or for two or more crimes to which it attaches a lighter penalty. Unlike recidivism, the previous offenses need not belong to the same title of the Code, but the offender must have served the sentences.
alac.application: Here, Vito was previously punished for serious physical injuries, whose penalty (prision correccional) is equal to that for the theft now charged. That alone satisfies the first part. He was also punished for slander, but that is not needed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, reiteracion aggravates Vito's liability for the theft.

keyPoints: Reiteracion (Art. 14(10))
Previous punishment for an offense with an equal or greater penalty, or two or more with lighter penalties
Crimes need not be in the same title
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 14(10)

q: Under Article 62 of the Revised Penal Code, a person is a habitual delinquent if, within ten years from his release or last conviction of the crimes of robo, hurto, estafa, or falsification:
choices: He is found guilty of any of said crimes a third time or oftener
hints: The crimes are limited to robo (robbery), hurto (theft), estafa and falsification.
It results in an additional penalty.
why: RPC Art. 62(5): habitual delinquency (third conviction or more within ten years of the listed crimes) results in additional penalties that increase with each conviction, the total not exceeding 30 years.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 62

q: Wilma was convicted of theft in 2016 and released in 2017, convicted of estafa in 2020 and released in 2021, and is now convicted of falsification in 2025. What is the effect on her penalty?

alac.answer: Wilma is a habitual delinquent, and an additional penalty must be imposed for her third conviction.
alac.basis: Article 62 of the Revised Penal Code provides that a person shall be deemed to be habitual delinquent if within a period of ten years from the date of his release or last conviction of the crimes of robo, hurto, estafa, or falsification, he is found guilty of any of said crimes a third time or oftener. Upon a third conviction, the culprit shall be sentenced to the penalty for the last crime and to the additional penalty of prision correccional in its medium and maximum periods.
alac.application: Here, Wilma's convictions for theft (hurto), estafa and falsification each came within ten years of her release or last conviction for the previous one. Her 2025 conviction for falsification is her third.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she must be sentenced to the penalty for falsification plus the additional penalty of prision correccional in its medium and maximum periods.

keyPoints: Habitual delinquency (Art. 62)
Third conviction within ten years of the listed crimes
Additional penalty for the third conviction
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 62

q: Under Article 25 of the Revised Penal Code, which of the following is an afflictive penalty?
hints: Afflictive: reclusion perpetua, reclusion temporal, disqualifications, prision mayor.
Correctional: prision correccional, arresto mayor, suspension, destierro.
why: RPC Art. 25 classifies principal penalties into capital, afflictive, correctional and light, plus fines and bond to keep the peace common to all, and lists accessory penalties.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 25

q: An accused was sentenced to destierro for a crime. He argues that destierro is a light penalty, so the crime prescribes in two months. How is destierro classified?

alac.answer: Destierro is a correctional penalty, not a light penalty.
alac.basis: Article 25 of the Revised Penal Code lists the correctional penalties as prision correccional, arresto mayor, suspension, and destierro, and the light penalties as arresto menor and public censure. The classification matters for prescription (Articles 90 and 92) and other rules.
alac.application: Here, destierro is expressly listed as a correctional penalty. The accused's characterization of it as a light penalty is wrong, so the rules for correctional penalties govern.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, destierro is a correctional penalty, and the prescriptive periods for crimes punished by correctional penalties apply.

keyPoints: Classification of penalties (Art. 25)
Destierro is correctional
Classification affects prescription
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 25

q: Under Article 40 of the Revised Penal Code, the death penalty, when not executed by reason of commutation or pardon, carries with it:
choices: Perpetual absolute disqualification and civil interdiction for thirty years, unless expressly remitted in the pardon
hints: Accessory penalties follow the principal penalty.
They may be remitted expressly by pardon.
why: RPC Arts. 40-45 attach accessory penalties to principal penalties (e.g., civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification for reclusion perpetua and temporal; suspension of the right to hold office for lower penalties) and forfeiture of the instruments and proceeds of the crime.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 40-45

q: A convict sentenced to reclusion perpetua for murder received a pardon from the President that did not mention any accessory penalty. He then ran for mayor. Can he run?

alac.answer: No, unless the pardon expressly restored his right to hold public office.
alac.basis: Under Articles 40 to 41 of the Revised Penal Code, reclusion perpetua carries with it the accessory penalties of civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification, which the offender shall suffer even if pardoned as to the principal penalty, unless the same shall have been expressly remitted in the pardon. In Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 206666, January 21, 2015, the Supreme Court held that a pardon whose terms clearly restore civil and political rights removes the disqualification.
alac.application: Here, the convict's pardon covered the principal penalty but did not expressly remit the accessory penalty of perpetual absolute disqualification or restore his political rights.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he remains disqualified from running for public office unless the pardon expressly restores that right.

keyPoints: Accessory penalties follow reclusion perpetua (Arts. 40-41)
Not remitted unless expressly stated in the pardon
Risos-Vidal v. COMELEC
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 40-41; Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 206666, January 21, 2015

q: Under Article 27 of the Revised Penal Code, reclusion temporal lasts:
hints: Prision mayor: 6 years and 1 day to 12 years.
Reclusion perpetua: 20 years and 1 day to 40 years (RA 7659), but remains indivisible.
why: RPC Art. 27: reclusion temporal 12y1d-20y; prision mayor 6y1d-12y; prision correccional 6m1d-6y; arresto mayor 1m1d-6m; arresto menor 1-30 days. Reclusion perpetua is 20y1d-40y under RA 7659 but remains indivisible (People v. Lucas, G.R. No. 108172, May 25, 1994).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 27; People v. Lucas, G.R. No. 108172, May 25, 1994

q: A trial court sentenced an accused to "reclusion perpetua, in its maximum period of 35 years." Is the sentence correct?

alac.answer: No; reclusion perpetua is an indivisible penalty and must be imposed simply as reclusion perpetua, without periods.
alac.basis: Article 27 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 7659, gives reclusion perpetua a duration of twenty years and one day to forty years. In People v. Lucas, G.R. No. 108172, May 25, 1994, the Supreme Court held that despite this fixed duration, reclusion perpetua remains an indivisible penalty, so it cannot be divided into periods.
alac.application: Here, the court divided reclusion perpetua into periods and fixed it at 35 years as its maximum period, treating it as divisible.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sentence should be corrected to simply reclusion perpetua.

keyPoints: Duration of penalties (Art. 27)
Reclusion perpetua remains indivisible (People v. Lucas)
No periods for indivisible penalties
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 27; People v. Lucas, G.R. No. 108172, May 25, 1994

q: Under Article 64 of the Revised Penal Code, for a divisible penalty with three periods, when there are neither aggravating nor mitigating circumstances, the court imposes:
hints: One mitigating: minimum period; one aggravating: maximum period.
Two or more mitigating and no aggravating: one degree lower.
why: RPC Art. 64: no circumstances: medium period; only mitigating: minimum; only aggravating: maximum; both: offset; two or more mitigating and no aggravating: penalty next lower. Art. 61 governs graduation by degrees.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 61 and 64

q: An accused convicted of homicide (reclusion temporal) had two mitigating circumstances, voluntary surrender and plea of guilty, and no aggravating circumstance. What penalty range should the court use?

alac.answer: The court should impose the penalty next lower in degree, prision mayor, in the period proper under Article 64.
alac.basis: Article 64 of the Revised Penal Code sets the rules for penalties with three periods: when there are neither aggravating nor mitigating circumstances, the medium period; when only a mitigating circumstance is present, the minimum period; and when there are two or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance, the court shall impose the penalty next lower to that prescribed by law, in the period it deems applicable. Article 61 provides how the next lower penalty is determined.
alac.application: Here, homicide is punished by reclusion temporal. There are two mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance, so the penalty is lowered by one degree to prision mayor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should impose prision mayor (with the Indeterminate Sentence Law then applied to fix the minimum and maximum).

keyPoints: Rules for penalties with three periods (Art. 64)
Two or more mitigating, no aggravating: one degree lower
Graduation by degrees (Art. 61)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 61 and 64

q: Under Section 2 of the Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103), the law does NOT apply to:
choices: A first offender sentenced to prision mayor
Persons convicted of offenses punished with death or life imprisonment, habitual delinquents, and those whose maximum term does not exceed one year, among others
hints: The ISLaw sets a minimum and a maximum term.
Parole may be granted after serving the minimum.
why: Act 4103: for RPC offenses, the maximum is the penalty properly imposable under the RPC rules, and the minimum is within the range of the penalty next lower; for special laws, within the range fixed by the law. Sec. 2 lists exclusions, including death or life imprisonment, treason, habitual delinquents, escapees, violators of conditional pardon, and maximum terms not exceeding one year.
cite: Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103, as amended), Secs. 1-2

q: Abel, a first offender, was convicted of homicide (reclusion temporal) with no modifying circumstances. The court sentenced him to a straight term of 14 years. Is the sentence correct?

alac.answer: No; the court should have imposed an indeterminate sentence.
alac.basis: Section 1 of the Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103) provides that where the offense is punished by the Revised Penal Code, the court shall sentence the accused to such maximum as may, in view of the attending circumstances, be properly imposed under the rules of the Code, and to a minimum within the range of the penalty next lower to that prescribed for the offense. Section 2 lists the persons excluded, none of which applies to a first offender convicted of homicide.
alac.application: Here, homicide is punished by reclusion temporal. With no modifying circumstances, the maximum is taken from the medium period of reclusion temporal (14 years, 8 months and 1 day to 17 years and 4 months), and the minimum from the penalty next lower, prision mayor (6 years and 1 day to 12 years).
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should impose an indeterminate sentence, for example 10 years of prision mayor as minimum to 14 years, 8 months and 1 day of reclusion temporal as maximum.

keyPoints: ISLaw applies to RPC offenses (Act 4103, Sec. 1)
Maximum: properly imposable under RPC rules; minimum: within the next lower penalty
Exclusions in Sec. 2
cite: Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103, as amended), Secs. 1-2

q: Under RA 9346, in lieu of the death penalty, the court shall impose:
choices: Reclusion perpetua, when the law uses RPC nomenclature, or life imprisonment, when it does not
hints: Persons so sentenced are not eligible for parole.
The death penalty is prohibited, not abolished from the Constitution.
why: RA 9346 prohibits the imposition of the death penalty and substitutes reclusion perpetua (if the law uses RPC nomenclature) or life imprisonment (if not); persons so sentenced are not eligible for parole under the ISLaw.
cite: RA 9346, Secs. 2-3

q: Bart was convicted of qualified rape, for which the law prescribes death. The court imposed reclusion perpetua "with eligibility for parole after 30 years." Is the sentence correct?

alac.answer: No; the court correctly imposed reclusion perpetua in lieu of death, but Bart is not eligible for parole.
alac.basis: RA 9346 prohibits the imposition of the death penalty and provides that, in lieu thereof, reclusion perpetua shall be imposed when the law violated uses the nomenclature of the penalties of the Revised Penal Code, or life imprisonment when it does not. Section 3 provides that persons convicted of offenses punished with reclusion perpetua, or whose sentences are reduced to reclusion perpetua by reason of the Act, shall not be eligible for parole under the Indeterminate Sentence Law.
alac.application: Here, the RPC prescribes death for qualified rape, so under RA 9346 the proper penalty is reclusion perpetua. But Bart's penalty was reduced to reclusion perpetua by reason of RA 9346, so he is not eligible for parole.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sentence should be reclusion perpetua "without eligibility for parole."

keyPoints: Death penalty prohibited (RA 9346)
Reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment in lieu
No parole eligibility (Sec. 3)
cite: RA 9346, Secs. 2-3

q: Under Article 39 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10159, subsidiary personal liability for an unpaid fine is computed at the rate of one day for each amount equivalent to:
choices: The highest minimum wage rate prevailing in the Philippines at the time of the trial court's judgment
hints: Subsidiary imprisonment applies only to fines.
It cannot exceed one-third of the principal penalty, and not more than one year in some cases.
why: RPC Art. 39, as amended by RA 10159: a convict without property to pay the fine suffers subsidiary personal liability at one day per amount equal to the highest minimum wage at the time of judgment, subject to limits (e.g., not exceeding one-third of the principal penalty and not more than one year for prision correccional or arresto and fine).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 39, as amended by RA 10159

q: Cora was sentenced to 4 months of arresto mayor and a fine, and to pay civil indemnity to the victim. She has no property. The court ordered subsidiary imprisonment for both the unpaid fine and the unpaid civil indemnity. Is the order correct?

alac.answer: No; subsidiary imprisonment may be imposed only for the unpaid fine, not for the civil indemnity.
alac.basis: Article 39 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10159, provides that if the convict has no property with which to meet the fine mentioned in paragraph 3 of Article 38, he shall be subject to a subsidiary personal liability at the rate of one day for each amount equivalent to the highest minimum wage rate prevailing at the time of judgment, and that if the principal penalty is arresto and fine, the subsidiary imprisonment shall not exceed one-third of the term of the sentence.
alac.application: Here, Cora has no property. The amended Article 39 limits subsidiary imprisonment to the fine; the civil indemnity is not covered. Since her principal penalty is 4 months of arresto mayor, her subsidiary imprisonment cannot exceed one-third of it, about 40 days.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the order should be modified to impose subsidiary imprisonment only for the unpaid fine, within the one-third limit.

keyPoints: Subsidiary penalty for unpaid fine only (Art. 39, as amended by RA 10159)
Rate based on the highest minimum wage
Limit: one-third of the principal penalty
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 39, as amended by RA 10159

q: Under Article 88a of the Revised Penal Code, inserted by RA 11362, community service may be required in lieu of service in jail for:
hints: The court has discretion.
Violation of the conditions means serving the jail term.
why: RPC Art. 88a (RA 11362, Community Service Act): the court may, in its discretion, require community service in the place where the crime was committed in lieu of jail for arresto menor and arresto mayor, under supervision; AM 20-06-14-SC provides the guidelines.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 88a (RA 11362)

q: Dino, a first offender, was convicted of slight physical injuries and sentenced to 20 days of arresto menor. He asked to render community service instead. Separately, Ella, sentenced to 2 years of prision correccional, made the same request. May the court grant them?

alac.answer: The court may grant Dino's request, but not Ella's.
alac.basis: Article 88a of the Revised Penal Code, inserted by RA 11362, provides that the court in its discretion may, in lieu of service in jail, require that the penalties of arresto menor and arresto mayor be served by the defendant by rendering community service in the place where the crime was committed, under such terms as the court shall determine. The policy is to promote restorative justice and decongest jails.
alac.application: Here, Dino's penalty is arresto menor, which may be served through community service at the court's discretion. Ella's penalty is prision correccional, which is not covered by Article 88a.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court may allow Dino to render community service, but Ella must serve her sentence (unless she qualifies for probation).

keyPoints: Community service in lieu of jail (Art. 88a, RA 11362)
Only for arresto menor and arresto mayor
Court's discretion
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 88a (RA 11362)

q: Under Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code, when a convict has to serve two or more penalties:
choices: He serves them simultaneously if their nature permits; otherwise, successively in the order of their severity
hints: Imprisonment penalties cannot be served simultaneously.
The threefold rule limits the total.
why: RPC Art. 70: penalties are served simultaneously if their nature permits (e.g., imprisonment and disqualification); otherwise successively, in the order of severity (death, reclusion perpetua, reclusion temporal, prision mayor, prision correccional, arresto mayor, arresto menor, destierro...).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 70

q: Fidel was sentenced in separate cases to prision correccional for theft and to prision mayor for robbery, plus perpetual special disqualification. In what order and manner should he serve these penalties?

alac.answer: He serves prision mayor first, then prision correccional, successively; the disqualification is served simultaneously.
alac.basis: Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code provides that when the culprit has to serve two or more penalties, he shall serve them simultaneously if the nature of the penalties will so permit; otherwise, they shall be executed successively, following the order of their respective severity: death, reclusion perpetua, reclusion temporal, prision mayor, prision correccional, arresto mayor, arresto menor, and so on.
alac.application: Here, two penalties of imprisonment cannot be served at the same time, so they are served successively, starting with the more severe, prision mayor, then prision correccional. The disqualification can be served at the same time as imprisonment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fidel serves prision mayor, then prision correccional, while the disqualification runs simultaneously, subject to the threefold rule.

keyPoints: Simultaneous service if nature permits (Art. 70)
Otherwise successive, in the order of severity
Disqualification may run with imprisonment
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 70

q: Under the threefold rule in Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code, the maximum duration of a convict's sentence:
choices: Shall not exceed three times the most severe penalty imposed, and in no case more than forty years
Is the sum of all penalties
hints: The rule applies to service, not to imposition.
Courts impose all penalties; the limit applies during service.
why: RPC Art. 70 (threefold rule): the maximum duration of the convict's sentence shall not be more than three times the length of the most severe penalty imposed, and such maximum shall not exceed forty years. It applies in the service, not the imposition, of the penalties.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 70

q: Gary was convicted in five separate cases and sentenced to 6 years in each (prision correccional), a total of 30 years. How many years must he actually serve?

alac.answer: Gary must serve 18 years under the threefold rule.
alac.basis: Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code provides the threefold rule: the maximum duration of the convict's sentence shall not be more than three times the length of time corresponding to the most severe of the penalties imposed upon him, and such maximum period shall in no case exceed forty years. The rule applies to the service, not the imposition, of the penalties.
alac.application: Here, the most severe single penalty is 6 years. Three times 6 years is 18 years, which is less than the 30-year total and less than forty years.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gary serves a maximum of 18 years, although the court must still impose all five penalties.

keyPoints: Threefold rule (Art. 70)
Three times the most severe penalty; maximum forty years
Applies to service, not imposition
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 70

q: Under the Probation Law, as amended by RA 10707, the benefits of probation do NOT extend to those:
choices: Sentenced to a maximum term of six years
Sentenced to serve a maximum term of imprisonment of more than six years
hints: Probation is a privilege, not a right.
As a rule, perfecting an appeal bars probation.
why: PD 968, as amended by RA 10707: the court may grant probation upon application within the period to appeal; no application if the appeal is perfected, except when the appellate court reduces a non-probationable penalty to a probationable one; disqualified are those sentenced to more than six years, convicted of crimes against national security, with prior conviction of more than six months and one day or fine over P1,000, or previously on probation.
cite: Probation Law (PD 968, as amended by RA 10707), Secs. 4 and 9

q: Hugo was convicted of frustrated homicide and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty with a maximum above six years. He appealed. The appellate court found only attempted homicide and reduced the penalty to a maximum of 4 years. May Hugo now apply for probation?

alac.answer: Yes, Hugo may apply for probation.
alac.basis: Section 4 of the Probation Law, as amended by RA 10707, provides that no application for probation shall be entertained if the defendant has perfected an appeal, but that when a judgment of conviction imposing a non-probationable penalty is appealed or reviewed, and the judgment is modified to a probationable penalty, the defendant may apply for probation based on the modified decision. This codifies Colinares v. People, G.R. No. 182748, December 13, 2011. Section 9 disqualifies those sentenced to a maximum term of imprisonment of more than six years.
alac.application: Here, Hugo's original penalty was non-probationable, so he could not have applied for probation before appealing. The appellate court reduced it to a maximum of 4 years, which is probationable.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Hugo may apply for probation on the basis of the modified decision, if he has no other disqualification.

keyPoints: Appeal generally bars probation (Sec. 4)
Exception: penalty reduced on appeal to a probationable one (RA 10707; Colinares v. People)
Disqualification: maximum term over six years (Sec. 9)
cite: Probation Law (PD 968, as amended by RA 10707), Secs. 4 and 9; Colinares v. People, G.R. No. 182748, December 13, 2011

q: Under Article 29 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10592, a detainee who agrees in writing to abide by the disciplinary rules for convicted prisoners is credited with:
choices: The full time of his preventive imprisonment
hints: Without the written agreement, he gets four-fifths.
Recidivists and those who fail to surrender are excluded.
why: RPC Art. 29, as amended by RA 10592: full credit of preventive imprisonment if the detainee agrees in writing, with counsel, to abide by the disciplinary rules for convicts; otherwise four-fifths; exceptions include recidivists and those who failed to surrender voluntarily for execution of sentence.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 29, as amended by RA 10592

q: Ivan was detained for 2 years during trial. He refused to sign the agreement to abide by the disciplinary rules for convicts. He was later convicted and sentenced to 6 years. How much of his detention is credited?

alac.answer: Ivan is credited with four-fifths of his preventive imprisonment.
alac.basis: Article 29 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10592, provides that offenders who have undergone preventive imprisonment shall be credited with the full time of their preventive imprisonment if they agree voluntarily in writing, with the assistance of counsel, to abide by the same disciplinary rules imposed upon convicted prisoners; if they do not agree, they shall be credited with four-fifths of the time of their preventive imprisonment, except for recidivists and other excluded persons.
alac.application: Here, Ivan did not agree in writing to abide by the disciplinary rules, so he does not get full credit. He is not shown to be a recidivist or otherwise excluded.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, four-fifths of his 2 years, about 19.2 months, is credited to his 6-year sentence.

keyPoints: Credit for preventive imprisonment (Art. 29, as amended by RA 10592)
Full credit with written agreement; four-fifths without
Exceptions such as recidivists
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 29, as amended by RA 10592

q: Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, the death of the accused before final judgment:
choices: Extinguishes criminal liability and the civil liability based solely on the offense
hints: Civil liability from other sources (e.g., quasi-delict, contract) survives.
People v. Bayotas states the rules.
why: RPC Art. 89(1): death of the convict extinguishes personal penalties, and pecuniary penalties only if death occurs before final judgment. Death pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto, but civil liability based on other sources survives and may be pursued in a separate action (People v. Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 89; People v. Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994

q: Jun was convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and ordered to pay damages. He died while his appeal was pending. The victim's heirs want to collect the damages from his estate in the same case. May they?

alac.answer: No; the criminal case and the civil liability arising from the crime are extinguished, but the heirs may file a separate civil action based on another source, such as quasi-delict.
alac.basis: Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code provides that criminal liability is totally extinguished by the death of the convict as to the personal penalties, and as to pecuniary penalties, only when the death occurs before final judgment. In People v. Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994, the Supreme Court held that the death of the accused pending appeal extinguishes his criminal liability and the civil liability based solely on the offense, but the claim for civil liability may survive if it is also based on another source of obligation, such as law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict, and must be pursued in a separate civil action against the estate.
alac.application: Here, Jun died pending appeal, before final judgment. His criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto are extinguished. But his negligent act may also be a quasi-delict.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the heirs cannot collect in the criminal case, but they may file a separate civil action against Jun's estate based on quasi-delict.

keyPoints: Death before final judgment extinguishes criminal and civil liability ex delicto (Art. 89(1))
Civil liability from other sources survives (People v. Bayotas)
Separate civil action against the estate
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 89; People v. Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994

q: Under Article 89(2) of the Revised Penal Code, criminal liability is totally extinguished:
hints: Service of sentence ends criminal liability.
Civil liability continues (Art. 113).
why: RPC Art. 89(2): service of sentence totally extinguishes criminal liability; but under Art. 113, the offender remains obliged to satisfy the civil liability.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89 and 113

q: Karl served his full sentence for estafa but never paid the P500,000 civil indemnity awarded to the victim. After his release, he argues that his liability was fully extinguished by service of sentence. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; service of sentence extinguished his criminal liability, but not his civil liability.
alac.basis: Article 89(2) of the Revised Penal Code provides that criminal liability is totally extinguished by service of the sentence. However, Article 113 provides that, except in case of extinction of civil liability under Article 112, the offender shall continue to be obliged to satisfy the civil liability resulting from the crime, notwithstanding the fact that he has served his sentence.
alac.application: Here, Karl's service of sentence ended his criminal liability. But his obligation to pay the P500,000 civil indemnity has not been extinguished by payment or any other mode under the Civil Code.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the victim may still enforce the civil indemnity against Karl.

keyPoints: Service of sentence extinguishes criminal liability (Art. 89(2))
Civil liability survives (Art. 113)
Extinguished only as other obligations (Art. 112)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89, 112 and 113

q: Amnesty, under Article 89(3) of the Revised Penal Code:
choices: Is granted by the President alone to a single convict
Completely extinguishes the penalty and all its effects, and is usually granted to classes of persons for political offenses, with the concurrence of Congress
Does not affect the criminal record
hints: Amnesty looks backward and abolishes the offense.
Pardon looks forward and relieves the offender of the consequences.
why: RPC Art. 89(3): amnesty completely extinguishes the penalty and all its effects. Amnesty is granted by the President with the concurrence of a majority of Congress (Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19), usually to classes of persons for political offenses, may be granted before or after conviction, and obliterates the offense (Barrioquinto v. Fernandez, G.R. No. L-1278, January 21, 1949).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 89; Barrioquinto v. Fernandez, G.R. No. L-1278, January 21, 1949

q: Leo, a rebel, was charged with rebellion and was still on trial when a presidential proclamation, concurred in by Congress, granted amnesty to all rebels who surrender within a period. Leo applied and was granted amnesty. Later, he was charged with rebellion again for the same acts. What is the effect of the amnesty?

alac.answer: The amnesty extinguished Leo's criminal liability for the rebellion, even before conviction, and he cannot be prosecuted again for the same acts.
alac.basis: Article 89(3) of the Revised Penal Code provides that criminal liability is totally extinguished by amnesty, which completely extinguishes the penalty and all its effects. In Barrioquinto v. Fernandez, G.R. No. L-1278, January 21, 1949, the Supreme Court explained that amnesty looks backward and abolishes the offense itself, as if the person had committed no offense, and that it may be granted before or after conviction, unlike pardon, which requires final conviction.
alac.application: Here, Leo was granted amnesty for rebellion while still on trial. The amnesty abolished the offense and all its effects.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the new charge for the same acts must be dismissed.

keyPoints: Amnesty extinguishes the penalty and all its effects (Art. 89(3))
May be granted before conviction
Amnesty v. pardon (Barrioquinto v. Fernandez)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 89; Barrioquinto v. Fernandez, G.R. No. L-1278, January 21, 1949

q: An absolute pardon by the President:
choices: Is granted only after conviction by final judgment and extinguishes criminal liability, but not the civil liability
hints: Pardon does not erase civil liability (Art. 113).
Accessory penalties remain unless expressly remitted.
why: RPC Art. 89(4): absolute pardon totally extinguishes criminal liability; under the Constitution (Art. VII, Sec. 19) it may be granted only after conviction by final judgment; it does not extinguish civil liability (Art. 113), and accessory penalties remain unless expressly remitted (Art. 36).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89 and 113

q: While Mina's appeal from a conviction for homicide was pending, the President granted her an absolute pardon. She also argues that the pardon wiped out the civil indemnity to the victim's heirs. Is the pardon valid, and what are its effects?

alac.answer: The pardon is not valid because Mina's conviction was not yet final; even a valid pardon would not erase the civil indemnity.
alac.basis: Article VII, Section 19 of the 1987 Constitution allows the President to grant pardons only after conviction by final judgment. Article 89(4) of the Revised Penal Code provides that absolute pardon totally extinguishes criminal liability, and Article 113 provides that the offender continues to be obliged to satisfy the civil liability notwithstanding pardon.
alac.application: Here, Mina's appeal was pending, so there was no conviction by final judgment; the pardon is premature. She may withdraw her appeal to let the judgment become final, and then be validly pardoned. In any case, a pardon would not extinguish her civil liability to the victim's heirs.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the pardon is ineffective as granted, and the civil indemnity remains due in all cases.

keyPoints: Pardon only after conviction by final judgment (Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19)
Absolute pardon extinguishes criminal liability (Art. 89(4))
Civil liability not extinguished (Art. 113)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89 and 113; 1987 Constitution, Art. VII, Sec. 19

q: Under Article 90 of the Revised Penal Code, crimes punishable by reclusion perpetua or reclusion temporal prescribe in:
hints: Other afflictive penalties: fifteen years; correctional: ten years; arresto mayor: five years.
Libel: two years (one year under RA 10175 debate aside).
why: RPC Art. 90 fixes prescription of crimes by penalty: 20 years (death, reclusion perpetua or temporal), 15 years (other afflictive), 10 years (correctional; 5 for arresto mayor), 2 years (libel), 6 months (oral defamation and slander by deed), 2 months (light offenses). Art. 91: counted from discovery, interrupted by filing the complaint.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 90 and 91

q: Noel committed estafa punishable by prision correccional in 2012, but the victim discovered it only in 2018. The complaint was filed with the prosecutor in 2027. Noel was abroad from 2019 to 2021. Has the crime prescribed?

alac.answer: No, the crime has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 90 of the Revised Penal Code provides that crimes punishable by a correctional penalty prescribe in ten years. Article 91 provides that the period of prescription commences to run from the day on which the crime is discovered by the offended party, the authorities or their agents, shall be interrupted by the filing of the complaint or information, and shall not run when the offender is absent from the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, the ten-year period began in 2018, upon discovery, not in 2012. It did not run during Noel's absence from 2019 to 2021, about two years. Counting from 2018 and adding the two years of absence, the period would end around 2030; the complaint filed in 2027 interrupted it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the crime has not prescribed.

keyPoints: Prescription periods by penalty (Art. 90)
Counted from discovery; interrupted by complaint (Art. 91)
Does not run while the offender is abroad
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 90 and 91

q: Under Act 3326, violations of special laws punished by imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years prescribe after:
hints: Act 3326 applies unless the special law provides otherwise.
Filing with the prosecutor interrupts the period (Panaguiton v. DOJ).
why: Act 3326 Sec. 1: special-law offenses prescribe after 1 year (fine or up to one month), 4 years (more than one month but less than two years), 8 years (two years or more but less than six), and 12 years (six years or more). Sec. 2: counted from commission (or discovery if unknown); interrupted by proceedings, including filing with the prosecutor (Panaguiton, Jr. v. Department of Justice, G.R. No. 167571, November 25, 2008).
cite: Act 3326, Secs. 1-2; Panaguiton, Jr. v. Department of Justice, G.R. No. 167571, November 25, 2008

q: Oscar issued bouncing checks in 1995; BP 22 punishes the offense by imprisonment of 30 days to one year. The victim filed a complaint with the prosecutor in 1997, but the information was filed in court only in 2003. Oscar argues that prescription ran until the case reached the court. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; the filing of the complaint with the prosecutor in 1997 interrupted the prescriptive period.
alac.basis: Section 1 of Act 3326 provides that offenses penalized by special acts, unless otherwise provided, prescribe after four years for those punished by imprisonment for more than one month but less than two years. Section 2 provides that prescription shall be interrupted when proceedings are instituted against the guilty person. In Panaguiton, Jr. v. Department of Justice, G.R. No. 167571, November 25, 2008, the Supreme Court held, in a BP 22 case, that the filing of the complaint with the prosecutor for preliminary investigation interrupts the prescriptive period under Act 3326.
alac.application: Here, the four-year period began in 1995 and was interrupted in 1997, when the complaint was filed with the prosecutor, well within four years. The delay before the information reached the court is not counted against the State.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the offense has not prescribed.

keyPoints: Prescription under special laws (Act 3326, Sec. 1)
Interrupted when proceedings are instituted (Sec. 2)
Filing with the prosecutor interrupts (Panaguiton v. DOJ)
cite: Act 3326, Secs. 1-2; Panaguiton, Jr. v. Department of Justice, G.R. No. 167571, November 25, 2008

q: Under Article 93 of the Revised Penal Code, the prescription of a penalty begins to run:
choices: From the date of the crime
From the date the culprit evades the service of his sentence
hints: The convict must have begun serving and then escaped.
It is interrupted if he goes to a country without an extradition treaty.
why: RPC Art. 92 sets periods for prescription of penalties (20, 15, 10, 5, 1 years). Art. 93: the period runs from evasion of service and is interrupted if the convict gives himself up, is captured, goes to a foreign country with no extradition treaty, or commits another crime. A convict who never began serving his sentence did not evade it (Del Castillo v. Torrecampo, G.R. No. 139033, December 18, 2002).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 92-93; Del Castillo v. Torrecampo, G.R. No. 139033, December 18, 2002

q: Pablo was convicted by final judgment and sentenced to prision correccional, but he hid and was never arrested to serve his sentence. Twelve years later, he argues that the penalty has prescribed. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; the penalty has not prescribed because Pablo never began serving his sentence, so he did not "evade" it.
alac.basis: Article 92 of the Revised Penal Code provides that correctional penalties prescribe in ten years. Article 93 provides that the period of prescription of penalties shall commence to run from the date when the culprit should evade the service of his sentence. In Del Castillo v. Torrecampo, G.R. No. 139033, December 18, 2002, the Supreme Court held that evasion of service of sentence presupposes escape during the service of the sentence; one who has not been committed to prison to serve his sentence cannot be said to have evaded it, so prescription of the penalty does not run.
alac.application: Here, Pablo hid after his conviction and was never detained to serve his sentence. He never began serving and so never escaped from service.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the prescription of the penalty has not begun to run, and Pablo may still be arrested to serve his sentence.

keyPoints: Prescription of penalties (Art. 92)
Runs from evasion of service (Art. 93)
No evasion without commencement of service (Del Castillo v. Torrecampo)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 92-93; Del Castillo v. Torrecampo, G.R. No. 139033, December 18, 2002

q: Under Article 344 of the Revised Penal Code, in cases of seduction, abduction and acts of lasciviousness, the marriage of the offender with the offended party:
choices: Extinguishes the criminal action or remits the penalty already imposed, and benefits co-principals, accomplices and accessories
hints: For rape under Art. 266-C, the subsequent valid marriage extinguishes the action or penalty, but not for co-principals.
The marriage must be in good faith, not a sham.
why: RPC Art. 89(7) and Art. 344: marriage of the offender with the offended party in seduction, abduction and acts of lasciviousness extinguishes the criminal action or remits the penalty, also benefiting co-principals, accomplices and accessories. For rape, Art. 266-C (RA 8353) applies, and the effect does not extend to co-principals.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89 and 344

q: Quinto, 25, was charged with qualified seduction of a 17-year-old. Before judgment, he married her in a valid, genuine marriage. His accomplice argues that the marriage benefits him too. Rule on the effect of the marriage.

alac.answer: The marriage extinguishes the criminal action against Quinto and also benefits his accomplice.
alac.basis: Article 89(7) of the Revised Penal Code provides that criminal liability is totally extinguished by the marriage of the offended woman, as provided in Article 344. Article 344 provides that in cases of seduction, abduction, acts of lasciviousness and rape, the marriage of the offender with the offended party shall extinguish the criminal action or remit the penalty already imposed, and that this shall also be applicable to the co-principals, accomplices and accessories after the fact. (For rape, the special rule of Article 266-C now governs.)
alac.application: Here, the crime is qualified seduction, and Quinto validly married the offended party in good faith. The marriage extinguishes the criminal action, and by the express terms of Article 344 its benefit extends to his accomplice.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the case must be dismissed as to both Quinto and the accomplice.

keyPoints: Marriage of offender and offended party (Arts. 89(7) and 344)
Extinguishes the action or remits the penalty
Benefits co-principals, accomplices and accessories in seduction
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89 and 344

q: Under Article 95 of the Revised Penal Code, a convict granted a conditional pardon who violates any of its conditions:
choices: Suffers revocation of the pardon and may be prosecuted under Article 159
hints: Conditional pardon partially extinguishes criminal liability.
The President may also order re-arrest without trial.
why: RPC Art. 94(1): conditional pardon partially extinguishes criminal liability; Art. 95: non-compliance results in revocation and the application of Art. 159 (evasion of service by violation of conditional pardon).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 94, 95 and 159

q: Rafael was granted a conditional pardon on the condition that he would not commit any crime. A year later, he was charged with theft. The President revoked the pardon and ordered his re-arrest, though he had not yet been convicted of the theft. Is the revocation valid?

alac.answer: Yes, the revocation and re-arrest are valid.
alac.basis: Article 95 of the Revised Penal Code provides that a person granted conditional pardon incurs the obligation of complying strictly with the conditions imposed, otherwise his non-compliance shall result in the revocation of the pardon. The determination of whether the conditions have been violated is an executive function; the President may revoke the pardon and order the re-arrest of the grantee without a judicial conviction for the new offense, apart from any prosecution under Article 159.
alac.application: Here, Rafael's pardon was conditioned on not committing any crime. The President, on the basis of the theft charge, determined that the condition was violated and revoked the pardon.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rafael may be re-arrested to serve the remainder of his sentence.

keyPoints: Conditional pardon partially extinguishes liability (Art. 94)
Violation results in revocation (Art. 95)
Executive determination; no conviction needed for revocation
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 94 and 95

q: Under Article 96 of the Revised Penal Code, commutation of sentence:
choices: Substitutes a lighter sentence of a different length or nature for the original one
hints: It partially extinguishes criminal liability.
The convict's consent is not needed.
why: RPC Arts. 94(2) and 96: commutation partially extinguishes criminal liability by substituting a lighter sentence for the original.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 94 and 96

q: Sergio's death sentence (imposed before RA 9346) was commuted by the President to reclusion perpetua. He argues that commutation is the same as an absolute pardon and that he should be released. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; commutation only substituted a lighter penalty, and he must serve reclusion perpetua.
alac.basis: Article 94 of the Revised Penal Code provides that criminal liability is partially extinguished by commutation of the sentence. Article 96 provides that the commutation of the original sentence for another of a different length and nature shall have the legal effect of substituting the latter in place of the former. Unlike absolute pardon, which totally extinguishes criminal liability (Article 89(4)), commutation only reduces the penalty.
alac.application: Here, the President commuted Sergio's death sentence to reclusion perpetua. The new penalty replaces the old one; it does not release him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sergio must serve the commuted penalty of reclusion perpetua.

keyPoints: Commutation partially extinguishes liability (Art. 94)
Substitutes the new sentence for the old (Art. 96)
Different from absolute pardon
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 94 and 96

q: Under Article 97 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10592, during the first two years of imprisonment, a prisoner with good behavior is allowed a deduction of:
choices: Twenty days for each month of good behavior
hints: The deduction increases in later years.
GCTA once granted is not revocable.
why: RPC Art. 97, as amended by RA 10592: GCTA of 20 days per month (first two years), 23 days (3rd-5th year), 25 days (6th-10th year), 30 days (11th year onward), plus 15 days per month for study, teaching or mentoring; it also applies to qualified detention prisoners.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by RA 10592

q: Tess, a detention prisoner during trial, agreed in writing to abide by the rules for convicted prisoners and behaved well. After conviction, the jail refused to count good conduct time for her detention period, saying GCTA applies only to convicted prisoners. Is the jail correct?

alac.answer: No; under RA 10592, good conduct time allowance also applies to qualified detention prisoners.
alac.basis: Article 97 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 10592, provides that the good conduct of any offender qualified for credit for preventive imprisonment pursuant to Article 29, or of any convicted prisoner in any penal institution, rehabilitation or detention center or any other local jail, shall entitle him to deductions from the period of his sentence, such as twenty days for each month of good behavior during the first two years.
alac.application: Here, Tess qualified for full credit for preventive imprisonment under Article 29 because she agreed in writing to abide by the disciplinary rules, and she behaved well in detention.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, her good conduct during detention must be credited as GCTA.

keyPoints: GCTA under Art. 97, as amended by RA 10592
Applies to detention prisoners qualified under Art. 29
Deduction rates by year of imprisonment
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by RA 10592

q: Under the Indeterminate Sentence Law, a prisoner may be released on parole:
choices: After serving the minimum of his indeterminate sentence, at the discretion of the Board of Pardons and Parole
hints: Parole is a privilege, not a right.
Those sentenced to reclusion perpetua by reason of RA 9346 are not eligible.
why: Act 4103 Sec. 1: a person convicted and sentenced under the ISLaw who has served the minimum sentence may be released on parole; it partially suspends the service of sentence, subject to conditions, and is not available to those excluded by Sec. 2 or by RA 9346.
cite: Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103, as amended), Sec. 1

q: Ursula is serving an indeterminate sentence of 6 years (minimum) to 10 years (maximum) for homicide. After 6 years, she applied for parole. Separately, Victor, sentenced to reclusion perpetua for murder, applied for parole after 30 years. Who may be granted parole?

alac.answer: Ursula may be considered for parole; Victor is not eligible.
alac.basis: Section 1 of the Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103) provides that any person convicted and sentenced under it who has served the minimum sentence may be released on parole. Section 2 provides that the law does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with death or life imprisonment, and Section 3 of RA 9346 provides that persons convicted of offenses punished with reclusion perpetua are not eligible for parole.
alac.application: Here, Ursula has served the 6-year minimum of her indeterminate sentence, so the Board of Pardons and Parole may consider her for parole. Victor's penalty is reclusion perpetua, which is excluded from parole.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, only Ursula may be paroled, at the Board's discretion; Victor may seek executive clemency instead.

keyPoints: Parole after serving the minimum (Act 4103, Sec. 1)
Exclusions (Sec. 2)
No parole for reclusion perpetua (RA 9346, Sec. 3)
cite: Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103, as amended), Secs. 1-2; RA 9346, Sec. 3

q: Under Article 103 of the Revised Penal Code, employers engaged in any kind of industry are subsidiarily liable for felonies committed by their employees:
choices: In the discharge of their duties, when the employee is insolvent
hints: Primary liability is on the offender (Art. 100).
Subsidiary liability requires conviction and insolvency of the employee.
why: RPC Art. 100: every person criminally liable is civilly liable; Arts. 102-103: innkeepers and employers are subsidiarily liable for crimes of their employees in the discharge of duties, enforceable upon the employee's conviction and insolvency.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 100-103

q: A bus driver was convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in homicide while driving for a bus company, and was ordered to pay P1 million. The driver is insolvent. Can the victim's heirs collect from the bus company in the same criminal case?

alac.answer: Yes, the heirs may enforce the bus company's subsidiary civil liability.
alac.basis: Article 100 of the Revised Penal Code provides that every person criminally liable for a felony is also civilly liable. Article 103 provides that employers and corporations engaged in any kind of industry are subsidiarily liable for felonies committed by their employees in the discharge of their duties. The subsidiary liability may be enforced in the same case upon the conviction of the employee and proof of his insolvency, the other requisites being that the employer is engaged in an industry and the employee committed the felony in the discharge of his duties.
alac.application: Here, the driver was convicted of a felony committed while driving for the bus company, an industry, and he is insolvent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the heirs may move for a writ of execution against the bus company on its subsidiary liability for the P1 million.

keyPoints: Primary civil liability of the offender (Art. 100)
Subsidiary liability of employers in industry (Art. 103)
Requisites: conviction, insolvency, discharge of duties
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 100 and 103

q: Under Article 104 of the Revised Penal Code, civil liability ex delicto includes:
choices: Restitution, reparation of the damage caused, and indemnification for consequential damages
hints: Restitution returns the thing itself.
Indemnification may include losses of the family or third persons (Art. 107).
why: RPC Art. 104: civil liability includes restitution, reparation and indemnification for consequential damages; Art. 105: restitution of the thing itself, even from a third person, without prejudice to his remedies; Art. 107: indemnification covers damages to the family and third persons.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 104-107

q: Wendy stole a car and sold it to a buyer who did not know it was stolen. Wendy was convicted. The owner wants the car back from the buyer, plus compensation for the car's damage and his lost income from his taxi business while the car was missing. What may he recover?

alac.answer: The owner may recover the car itself (restitution), compensation for its damage (reparation), and his lost income (indemnification for consequential damages).
alac.basis: Article 104 of the Revised Penal Code provides that civil liability includes restitution, reparation of the damage caused, and indemnification for consequential damages. Restitution of the thing itself must be made whenever possible, even if it is in the possession of a third person who acquired it by lawful means, saving to the latter his action against the proper person (Article 105). Indemnification for consequential damages includes those suffered by the injured party (Article 107).
alac.application: Here, the car can be recovered from the buyer, who may then proceed against Wendy. The damage to the car is covered by reparation, and the lost taxi income is a consequential damage resulting from the theft.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the owner may recover all three, with the buyer having recourse against Wendy.

keyPoints: Civil liability includes restitution, reparation and indemnification (Art. 104)
Restitution even from a good-faith third person (Art. 105)
Consequential damages (Art. 107)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 104-107

q: Under Article 101 of the Revised Penal Code, for acts committed by an insane person exempt from criminal liability, civil liability is borne:
choices: By those having legal authority or control over him, if they were at fault or negligent; otherwise by the insane person's own property
hints: Exemption from criminal liability does not mean exemption from civil liability.
In state of necessity, those benefited are liable.
why: RPC Art. 101: exemption from criminal liability under Art. 12 (pars. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6) and Art. 11(4) does not include civil liability; for insane persons and minors, those with legal authority or control are liable if negligent, otherwise the person's own property; in state of necessity, those benefited are liable in proportion to the benefit.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 101

q: To stop a spreading fire from reaching a whole village, Xavier, a barangay official, ordered the demolition of Yna's house, which saved twenty other houses. He is not criminally liable because of the state of necessity. Who must compensate Yna?

alac.answer: The owners of the houses that were saved must compensate Yna, in proportion to the benefit each received.
alac.basis: Article 11(4) of the Revised Penal Code exempts from criminal liability any person who, in order to avoid an evil or injury, does an act which causes damage to another, provided the evil actually exists, the injury feared is greater, and there is no other practical and less harmful means. Article 101 provides that this justification does not include exemption from civil liability, and that the persons for whose benefit the harm was prevented shall be civilly liable in proportion to the benefit they received.
alac.application: Here, Xavier's demolition of Yna's house was justified by state of necessity, so he is not criminally liable. The twenty houses were saved by the sacrifice of Yna's house, so their owners benefited.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the owners of the saved houses must compensate Yna in proportion to their benefit, as determined by the court.

keyPoints: State of necessity (Art. 11(4))
No exemption from civil liability (Art. 101)
Those benefited pay in proportion
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 11 and 101

q: Under Article 110 of the Revised Penal Code, the principals, accomplices and accessories of a felony are liable for civil liability:
choices: Equally, all solidarily for the whole
Severally (solidarily) within their respective class for their quotas, and subsidiarily for those of the other classes
hints: The court fixes the quota of each class (Art. 109).
Subsidiary liability is enforced first against the principals' property, then accomplices', then accessories'.
why: RPC Art. 109: the court fixes the share of each class (principals, accomplices, accessories); Art. 110: each class is solidarily liable for its quota, and subsidiarily for the quotas of the others, enforced first against the principals, then accomplices, then accessories.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 109-110

q: Two principals and one accomplice were convicted of homicide. The court ordered P600,000 civil indemnity: P400,000 for the principals and P200,000 for the accomplice. One principal is insolvent. How may the heirs collect?

alac.answer: The solvent principal must pay the full P400,000 quota of the principals, and the accomplice his P200,000; the accomplice is also subsidiarily liable for the principals' quota if they cannot pay.
alac.basis: Article 109 of the Revised Penal Code requires the court to determine the amount for which each class is liable. Article 110 provides that the principals, accomplices, and accessories, each within their respective class, shall be liable severally (in solidum) among themselves for their quotas, and subsidiarily for those of the other persons liable, the subsidiary liability being enforced first against the property of the principals, next against the accomplices, and lastly against the accessories.
alac.application: Here, the two principals are solidarily liable for their P400,000 quota, so the heirs may collect it all from the solvent principal, who may seek reimbursement from his co-principal. The accomplice answers for his P200,000 quota and, subsidiarily, for any unpaid part of the principals' quota.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the heirs may collect P400,000 from the solvent principal and P200,000 from the accomplice, with the accomplice's subsidiary liability as a fallback.

keyPoints: Court fixes quotas by class (Art. 109)
Solidary within each class, subsidiary for other classes (Art. 110)
Order of subsidiary enforcement
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 109-110

q: Under Article 38 of the Revised Penal Code, when the offender's property is not enough to cover all his pecuniary liabilities, which is paid first?
choices: The reparation of the damage caused
hints: The victim's reparation comes before the State's fine.
Order: reparation, indemnification, fine, costs.
why: RPC Art. 38: pecuniary liabilities are paid in this order: (1) reparation of the damage caused; (2) indemnification of consequential damages; (3) the fine; (4) the costs of the proceedings. The subsidiary liability of different classes is enforced in the order of Art. 110.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 38 and 110

q: Zandro was convicted of estafa and ordered to pay reparation of P300,000, consequential damages of P100,000, a fine of P50,000 and costs of P10,000. His only property was sold for P350,000. How should the proceeds be applied?

alac.answer: P300,000 goes to reparation and the remaining P50,000 to consequential damages; nothing is left for the fine and costs.
alac.basis: Article 38 of the Revised Penal Code provides that in case the property of the offender is not sufficient for the payment of all his pecuniary liabilities, they shall be met in the following order: (1) the reparation of the damage caused; (2) indemnification of consequential damages; (3) the fine; and (4) the costs of the proceedings.
alac.application: Here, the P350,000 is not enough for the total of P460,000. Applying the order of preference, the first P300,000 pays the reparation in full, and the remaining P50,000 goes to the consequential damages, leaving P50,000 of that item, the fine and the costs unpaid.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the proceeds are applied first to reparation and then to consequential damages, and the unpaid fine may give rise to subsidiary imprisonment under Article 39.

keyPoints: Order of payment of pecuniary liabilities (Art. 38)
Victim's reparation and damages before the fine and costs
Subsidiary imprisonment for unpaid fine (Art. 39)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 38 and 39

q: Under Article 112 of the Revised Penal Code, civil liability arising from a crime is extinguished:
choices: In the same manner as other obligations, in accordance with the Civil Code
hints: Civil liability survives service of sentence and pardon (Art. 113).
The obligation passes to the heirs of the person liable, up to the estate (Art. 108).
why: RPC Art. 112: civil liability is extinguished like other obligations (payment, condonation, compensation, prescription, etc.); Art. 113: it survives service of sentence, amnesty, pardon and commutation; Art. 108: the obligation devolves upon the heirs of the person liable, and the action descends to the heirs of the injured party.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 108, 112 and 113

q: Abner was convicted with finality of physical injuries and ordered to pay P200,000. The victim later signed a written waiver condoning the debt. Separately, another convict died after final judgment owing P500,000 in civil indemnity. What happens to each civil liability?

alac.answer: Abner's civil liability is extinguished by condonation; the deceased convict's civil liability survives and is charged against his estate.
alac.basis: Article 112 of the Revised Penal Code provides that civil liability shall be extinguished in the same manner as other obligations, in accordance with the Civil Code, which includes condonation or remission. Article 108 provides that the obligation to make restoration, reparation and indemnification devolves upon the heirs of the person liable. Under Article 89(1), the death of the convict extinguishes pecuniary liability only when it occurs before final judgment.
alac.application: Here, the victim condoned Abner's debt in writing, so his civil liability is extinguished. The other convict died after final judgment, so his civil liability survives and is paid from his estate, the heirs being liable only up to the value of what they inherit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Abner owes nothing more, while the P500,000 may be claimed against the deceased convict's estate.

keyPoints: Civil liability extinguished like other obligations (Art. 112)
Condonation extinguishes it
Survives death after final judgment; charged to the estate (Arts. 89(1), 108)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 89, 108 and 112

q: Under Article 114 of the Revised Penal Code, no person shall be convicted of treason unless:
choices: On the testimony of two witnesses at least to the same overt act, or on confession of the accused in open court
He is caught in the act
hints: This is the two-witness rule.
Treason requires allegiance, war, and adherence to the enemy with aid or comfort.
why: RPC Art. 114: treason is committed by one owing allegiance who levies war against the government or adheres to its enemies, giving them aid or comfort; conviction requires two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 114

q: During a war, Filipino citizen Ador supplied food and maps to enemy troops occupying his town. At his trial for treason, one witness saw him deliver the food, and another saw him deliver the maps on a different day. He made no confession. Can he be convicted of treason?

alac.answer: No, he cannot be convicted of treason on this evidence.
alac.basis: Article 114 of the Revised Penal Code punishes any person who, owing allegiance to the Government, adheres to its enemies, giving them aid or comfort, and provides that no person shall be convicted of treason unless on the testimony of two witnesses at least to the same overt act, or on confession of the accused in open court.
alac.application: Here, Ador's acts of supplying food and maps are overt acts of adherence and aid to the enemy. But each act was seen by only one witness; there are no two witnesses to the same overt act, and there is no confession in open court.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the two-witness rule is not satisfied, and Ador must be acquitted of treason.

keyPoints: Elements of treason (Art. 114)
Two-witness rule to the same overt act
Or confession in open court
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 114

q: Under Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by EO 272, a person lawfully arrested without a warrant for a crime punishable by afflictive or capital penalties must be delivered to the proper judicial authorities within:
hints: Light penalties: 12 hours; correctional: 18 hours; afflictive or capital: 36 hours.
'Delivery' means filing the complaint or information in court.
why: RPC Art. 125, as amended by EO 272: delay in the delivery of detained persons is committed by a public officer who detains a person for a legal ground and fails to deliver him to the judicial authorities within 12, 18 or 36 hours, depending on the penalty. Art. 124 punishes detention without legal ground (arbitrary detention).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 124-125, as amended by EO 272

q: Police officers lawfully arrested Bert without a warrant for robbery (an afflictive penalty) at 8:00 a.m. on Monday. They kept him at the station and filed the information in court only on Thursday at noon, without any justifiable reason. What crime did the officers commit?

alac.answer: The officers committed delay in the delivery of detained persons to the proper judicial authorities.
alac.basis: Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by EO 272, punishes a public officer who shall detain any person for some legal ground and shall fail to deliver such person to the proper judicial authorities within twelve hours for crimes punishable by light penalties, eighteen hours for correctional penalties, and thirty-six hours for afflictive or capital penalties. Delivery means the filing of the complaint or information in court. If the detention had no legal ground at all, the crime would be arbitrary detention under Article 124.
alac.application: Here, Bert's warrantless arrest was lawful, so there was a legal ground. Robbery carries an afflictive penalty, so the officers had 36 hours, until 8:00 p.m. on Tuesday, to file the case. They filed it only on Thursday, without justification.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the officers are liable for delay in the delivery of detained persons under Article 125.
