keyPoints: Delay in delivery: lawful detention, failure to deliver within the period (Art. 125, as amended)
12/18/36 hours depending on the penalty
Arbitrary detention if no legal ground (Art. 124)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 124-125, as amended by EO 272

q: Under Article 148 of the Revised Penal Code, direct assault includes:
choices: Attacking, employing force, seriously intimidating or resisting a person in authority or his agents while engaged in the performance of official duties or on occasion of such performance
hints: There must be no public uprising.
The offender must know the victim is a person in authority or agent.
why: RPC Art. 148: direct assault, without public uprising, by force or intimidation for purposes of rebellion or sedition, or by attacking or seriously intimidating or resisting a person in authority or agent engaged in official duties or on occasion thereof. Rebellion (Art. 134) requires a public uprising and taking arms against the government.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 134 and 148

q: A public school teacher, who is a person in authority while teaching, gave a student a failing grade. The next day, at the market and while off duty, the student's father punched her because of the grade. What crime did the father commit?

alac.answer: The father committed direct assault (complexed with physical injuries if any resulted).
alac.basis: Article 148 of the Revised Penal Code punishes any person who, without a public uprising, shall attack, employ force or seriously intimidate or resist any person in authority or any of his agents, while engaged in the performance of official duties, or on occasion of such performance. Teachers are persons in authority under the Code. "On occasion of" the performance of duties covers attacks made because of the official's past performance of duty, even if the official is no longer performing it.
alac.application: Here, the teacher was off duty at the market, but the father punched her because of the failing grade she gave, which is an attack on occasion of her performance of official duties.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the father is liable for direct assault, complexed with the resulting physical injuries.

keyPoints: Direct assault on persons in authority (Art. 148)
Teachers are persons in authority
'On occasion of' covers attacks because of past performance of duty
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 148

q: Under Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, falsification by a public officer requires that he:
choices: Takes advantage of his official position in falsifying a document by any of the acts listed
hints: The acts include imitating signatures and causing it to appear that persons participated when they did not.
Damage to a third party is not needed for public documents.
why: RPC Art. 171: a public officer, employee or notary who, taking advantage of his official position, falsifies a document by any listed act (counterfeiting signatures, attributing participation, untruthful statements of facts, etc.) commits falsification; Art. 183 punishes perjury: willful untruthful statements under oath on a material matter.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 171 and 183

q: Clara executed an affidavit before a notary, stating under oath that she had never been married, in order to obtain a business permit that required no such statement. In fact she was married. Is she liable for perjury?

alac.answer: No, Clara is not liable for perjury because the false statement was not on a material matter required by law.
alac.basis: Article 183 of the Revised Penal Code punishes any person who, knowingly making untruthful statements, shall testify under oath, or make an affidavit, upon any material matter before a competent person authorized to administer an oath in cases in which the law so requires. The elements are: a statement under oath or affidavit on a material matter, before a competent officer, a willful and deliberate assertion of a falsehood, and that the sworn statement is required by law.
alac.application: Here, Clara's statement was false and made under oath before a notary. But her civil status was not a material matter for the business permit, and no law required that sworn statement for that purpose.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the elements of perjury are not complete, and Clara cannot be convicted of perjury.

keyPoints: Elements of perjury (Art. 183)
Material matter
Sworn statement required by law
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 183

q: Under Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, the physical inventory and photographing of seized drugs must be done in the presence of the accused (or representative or counsel), and:
choices: An elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media
hints: Noncompliance may be excused on justifiable grounds if integrity is preserved.
The prosecution must explain any deviation (People v. Lim).
why: RA 9165 Sec. 21(1), as amended by RA 10640: immediately after seizure, inventory and photographs in the presence of the accused, an elected public official, and a representative of the NPS or media; noncompliance under justifiable grounds does not void the seizure if the integrity and evidentiary value are preserved, and the prosecution must prove the grounds (People v. Lim, G.R. No. 231989, September 4, 2018).
cite: Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act (RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640), Sec. 21; People v. Lim, G.R. No. 231989, September 4, 2018

q: After a buy-bust operation, police marked and inventoried the shabu at the station without any elected official, prosecutor or media representative present, giving no explanation. The forensic chemist confirmed the substance was shabu. Should the accused be convicted of illegal sale?

alac.answer: No, the accused should be acquitted because the chain of custody was broken without justification.
alac.basis: Section 21(1) of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, requires the apprehending team, immediately after seizure, to conduct a physical inventory and photograph the seized items in the presence of the accused, an elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media. Noncompliance under justifiable grounds, as long as the integrity and evidentiary value of the items are preserved, shall not render the seizure void. In People v. Lim, G.R. No. 231989, September 4, 2018, the Supreme Court required the prosecution to prove the presence of the required witnesses or to justify their absence and show earnest efforts to secure them.
alac.application: Here, none of the required witnesses was present, and the police offered no explanation. The integrity of the corpus delicti, the drugs, was not established beyond reasonable doubt, despite the chemist's findings.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the accused must be acquitted.

keyPoints: Inventory and photographs with required witnesses (Sec. 21, as amended by RA 10640)
Saving clause requires justifiable grounds
Prosecution must prove compliance or justification (People v. Lim)
cite: Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act (RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640), Sec. 21; People v. Lim, G.R. No. 231989, September 4, 2018

q: Under RA 9287, an illegal numbers game is:
choices: Any form of illegal gambling activity which uses numbers or combinations thereof as factors in giving out jackpots
hints: Jueteng, masiao and last two are examples.
RA 9287 increased penalties under PD 1602.
why: RPC Title VI (crimes against public morals) is excluded from the 2027 syllabus; illegal gambling is governed by PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287, which defines illegal numbers games and penalizes bettors, collectors, coordinators, financiers and protectors, with heavier penalties for public officials.
cite: PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287

q: A barangay captain received weekly payments from a jueteng operator in exchange for preventing police raids in his barangay. Under what law is he liable, and is his position relevant?

alac.answer: He is liable as a protector of an illegal numbers game under PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287, and his being a public official increases his liability.
alac.basis: PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287, penalizes illegal numbers games, defined as any form of illegal gambling activity which uses numbers or combinations thereof as factors in giving out jackpots, such as jueteng. It penalizes not only bettors and operators but also those who act as protectors or coddlers, and imposes higher penalties, including perpetual disqualification, on public officials who commit these acts.
alac.application: Here, jueteng is an illegal numbers game. The barangay captain received money to shield the operation from police raids, which makes him a protector. He is a public official.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable as a protector of an illegal numbers game, with the heavier penalties for public officials, aside from possible liability under anti-graft laws.

keyPoints: Illegal numbers game defined (RA 9287)
Liability of protectors or coddlers
Heavier penalty for public officials
cite: PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287

q: Under Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code, the failure of an accountable public officer to have duly forthcoming public funds upon demand:
choices: Is prima facie evidence that he has put the missing funds to personal uses
Is proof of theft by a third person
hints: Malversation can be committed through negligence.
The officer may rebut the presumption.
why: RPC Art. 217: an accountable public officer who appropriates, takes, misappropriates or, through abandonment or negligence, permits another to take public funds commits malversation; failure to produce the funds on demand is prima facie evidence of personal use. Art. 210 punishes direct bribery.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 210 and 217

q: A municipal treasurer left the vault open and unattended overnight, and P1 million in public funds was stolen by unknown persons. He had no part in the theft. Is he liable for malversation?

alac.answer: Yes, he is liable for malversation through negligence.
alac.basis: Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code punishes any public officer who, by reason of the duties of his office, is accountable for public funds or property, and who shall appropriate the same, or shall take or misappropriate, or shall consent, or through abandonment or negligence, shall permit any other person to take such public funds or property. Malversation may thus be committed intentionally or through negligence, and the mode is not an element that must be specifically alleged in a different way.
alac.application: Here, the treasurer is accountable for the funds. By leaving the vault open and unattended overnight, he negligently permitted others to take P1 million. That he did not take part in the theft does not matter.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable for malversation through negligence, with the penalty based on the amount involved under RA 10951.

keyPoints: Malversation by an accountable officer (Art. 217)
May be committed through abandonment or negligence
Penalty based on amount (as amended by RA 10951)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 217

q: Under Article 246 of the Revised Penal Code, parricide is committed by killing:
choices: One's father, mother, or child (legitimate or illegitimate), other legitimate ascendants or descendants, or one's spouse
hints: Relationship is the key element.
Killing with treachery a non-relative is murder (Art. 248).
why: RPC Art. 246: parricide is the killing of one's father, mother or child, whether legitimate or illegitimate, any of one's (legitimate) ascendants or descendants, or one's spouse; Art. 248: murder is the killing of another, not parricide, with qualifying circumstances such as treachery; Art. 249: homicide otherwise.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 246 and 248

q: Dario killed his common-law wife by shooting her from behind while she slept. What crime did he commit, parricide or murder?

alac.answer: Dario committed murder, not parricide.
alac.basis: Article 246 of the Revised Penal Code defines parricide as the killing of one's father, mother, or child, any of one's ascendants or descendants, or one's spouse; the relationship of spouse requires a valid marriage. Article 248 provides that any person who, not falling within Article 246, shall kill another with treachery shall be guilty of murder. There is treachery when the victim is attacked while asleep, unable to defend herself.
alac.application: Here, Dario and the victim were not married, so she was not his spouse, and the killing is not parricide. He shot her from behind while she slept, which is treachery.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dario is liable for murder qualified by treachery.

keyPoints: Parricide requires the listed relationships; spouse means a legal spouse (Art. 246)
Murder: killing qualified by treachery (Art. 248)
Attack on a sleeping victim is treacherous
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 246 and 248

q: Under Article 267 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 7659, kidnapping for ransom is committed when the kidnapping is for the purpose of extorting ransom:
choices: Only if the detention lasts more than three days
Even if none of the other qualifying circumstances (duration, simulated authority, injuries, minor victim) is present
Only if the victim is a minor
Only if ransom is actually paid
hints: Purpose of ransom alone suffices.
Death of the victim results in the special complex crime.
why: RPC Art. 267, as amended by RA 7659: kidnapping and serious illegal detention by a private individual, qualified by duration over three days, simulation of authority, serious physical injuries or threats to kill, or a minor victim; the penalty applies when the purpose is to extort ransom even if none of those circumstances is present; maximum penalty if the victim is killed, raped or tortured.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 267, as amended by RA 7659

q: Eman and his group seized a businessman and held him for six hours, demanding P5 million for his release. Police rescued him before any payment. The group argues that kidnapping requires detention of more than three days, and that no ransom was paid. Rule on their defenses.

alac.answer: Both defenses fail; they are liable for kidnapping for ransom.
alac.basis: Article 267 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 7659, punishes any private individual who shall kidnap or detain another, or in any other manner deprive him of his liberty, with reclusion perpetua to death if, among others, the detention lasted more than three days, and provides that the penalty shall be imposed when the kidnapping or detention was committed for the purpose of extorting ransom from the victim or any other person, even if none of the circumstances above-mentioned were present.
alac.application: Here, the group, private individuals, deprived the businessman of his liberty and demanded P5 million for his release, so the purpose was to extort ransom. The short duration does not matter, and the crime does not require actual payment of the ransom.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they are liable for kidnapping for ransom.

keyPoints: Kidnapping and serious illegal detention (Art. 267, as amended)
Purpose of extorting ransom suffices regardless of duration
Actual payment not required
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 267, as amended by RA 7659

q: What distinguishes robbery from theft under Articles 293 and 308 of the Revised Penal Code?
choices: Robbery is committed by means of violence against or intimidation of persons, or force upon things; theft is committed without them
hints: Both require taking personal property of another with intent to gain.
Estafa (Art. 315) involves deceit or abuse of confidence.
why: RPC Art. 293: robbery is taking personal property of another with intent to gain, by violence or intimidation of persons or force upon things; Art. 308: theft is taking without violence, intimidation or force upon things; Art. 315: estafa is defrauding another by abuse of confidence or deceit.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 293, 308 and 315

q: Fely, a house helper, took her employer's jewelry from an unlocked drawer and fled. Separately, Gelo broke the window of a house to enter and took a laptop. What crimes did they commit?

alac.answer: Fely committed qualified theft; Gelo committed robbery with force upon things.
alac.basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code provides that theft is committed by any person who, with intent to gain but without violence against or intimidation of persons nor force upon things, shall take personal property of another without the latter's consent; Article 310 qualifies theft when committed by a domestic servant or with grave abuse of confidence. Article 293 provides that robbery is the taking of personal property of another with intent to gain, by means of violence or intimidation of persons, or using force upon anything, such as entering a house by breaking a window (Article 299).
alac.application: Here, Fely took the jewelry without violence or force, from an unlocked drawer, as a domestic helper, so the theft is qualified. Gelo broke a window to enter the house and take the laptop, which is force upon things.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fely is liable for qualified theft, and Gelo for robbery in an inhabited house.

keyPoints: Theft: no violence, intimidation or force upon things (Art. 308)
Qualified theft by a domestic servant (Art. 310)
Robbery with force upon things (Arts. 293, 299)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 293, 299, 308 and 310

q: Under Article 333 of the Revised Penal Code, adultery is committed by:
choices: Any married man who has sexual intercourse with another woman
A married woman who has sexual intercourse with a man not her husband, and by the man who has carnal knowledge of her knowing her to be married
A married man keeping a mistress in the conjugal dwelling only
hints: Concubinage (Art. 334) is the crime of the married man, under specific circumstances.
Only the offended spouse may file the complaint, against both offenders (Art. 344).
why: RPC Art. 333: adultery by a married woman and her paramour who knows she is married, even if the marriage is later declared void; Art. 334: concubinage by a husband who keeps a mistress in the conjugal dwelling, has intercourse under scandalous circumstances, or cohabits with her elsewhere; Art. 344: prosecution only upon complaint of the offended spouse, against both guilty parties.
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 333, 334 and 344

q: Hector filed a complaint for adultery against his wife only, sparing her paramour, who was his business partner. Is the complaint proper?

alac.answer: No, the complaint is improper because it must include both guilty parties.
alac.basis: Article 344 of the Revised Penal Code provides that the crimes of adultery and concubinage shall not be prosecuted except upon a complaint filed by the offended spouse, and that the offended party cannot institute criminal prosecution without including both the guilty parties, if they are both alive, nor, in any case, if he shall have consented or pardoned the offenders. Article 333 defines adultery as committed by the married woman and by the man who has carnal knowledge of her knowing her to be married.
alac.application: Here, Hector filed the complaint against his wife only, though her paramour is alive and is equally a guilty party.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the complaint cannot prosper unless it includes both his wife and her paramour.

keyPoints: Adultery by the married woman and her paramour (Art. 333)
Complaint by the offended spouse against both guilty parties (Art. 344)
Consent or pardon bars prosecution
cite: Revised Penal Code, Arts. 333 and 344

q: Under Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code, bigamy is committed by a person who contracts a second marriage:
choices: Before the former marriage has been legally dissolved, or before the absent spouse has been declared presumptively dead by judgment
After annulment of the first marriage
hints: A judicial declaration of nullity of the first marriage is needed before remarrying (Family Code, Art. 40).
Later nullity of the second marriage is not a defense (Capili v. People).
why: RPC Art. 349: bigamy requires a valid first marriage not legally dissolved (or absent spouse not judicially declared presumptively dead) and a second marriage with all the essential requisites but for the first. The subsequent judicial declaration of nullity of the second marriage does not extinguish bigamy (Capili v. People, G.R. No. 183805, July 3, 2013).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 349; Capili v. People, G.R. No. 183805, July 3, 2013

q: While married to Ines, Jaime married Karen. Charged with bigamy, Jaime later obtained a judicial declaration that his marriage to Karen was void for lack of a marriage license. He moves to dismiss the bigamy case. Should it be dismissed?

alac.answer: No, the bigamy case should not be dismissed.
alac.basis: Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code punishes any person who shall contract a second or subsequent marriage before the former marriage has been legally dissolved. In Capili v. People, G.R. No. 183805, July 3, 2013, the Supreme Court held that the crime of bigamy is consummated upon the celebration of the second marriage while the first is subsisting, and that a subsequent judicial declaration of nullity of the second marriage does not affect the criminal liability already incurred.
alac.application: Here, Jaime married Karen while his marriage to Ines was subsisting. The bigamy was consummated at that moment. The later declaration that the second marriage was void does not erase the crime.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the motion to dismiss should be denied.

keyPoints: Elements of bigamy (Art. 349)
Consummated upon the second marriage
Later nullity of the second marriage is not a defense (Capili v. People)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 349; Capili v. People, G.R. No. 183805, July 3, 2013

q: Under Article 353 of the Revised Penal Code, libel is:
choices: Any criticism of a public official

A public and malicious imputation of a crime, vice or defect, real or imaginary, or any act, condition or circumstance tending to cause dishonor, discredit or contempt of a person, or to blacken the memory of one who is dead
hints: Elements: imputation, publication, identity, malice.
Cyberlibel under RA 10175 covers the original author (Disini v. Secretary of Justice).
why: RPC Art. 353 defines libel; malice is presumed except in privileged communications (Art. 354). Online libel by the original author is punishable under RA 10175, but not those who merely react to or share the post (Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 353; Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014

q: Lara posted on Facebook that her neighbor, a named teacher, "steals from the school canteen." The post was false. Mike only clicked "like" on it. Who is liable for cyberlibel?

alac.answer: Lara is liable for cyberlibel, but Mike is not.
alac.basis: Article 353 of the Revised Penal Code defines libel as a public and malicious imputation of a crime, or of a vice or defect, tending to cause the dishonor, discredit, or contempt of a person. The Cybercrime Prevention Act punishes libel committed through a computer system. In Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014, the Supreme Court upheld cyberlibel as applied to the original author of the defamatory post, but held that those who simply receive the post and react to it, such as by liking or commenting, are not liable.
alac.application: Here, Lara publicly imputed a crime, theft, to an identified teacher, falsely and on Facebook, satisfying the elements of libel through a computer system. Mike only liked the post, which is a mere reaction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lara may be prosecuted for cyberlibel, while Mike may not.

keyPoints: Libel defined (Art. 353)
Cyberlibel for the original author
No liability for merely liking or reacting (Disini v. Secretary of Justice)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 353; Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175); Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014

q: According to Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, a reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and damage to property, arising from one act:
choices: Constitutes a single quasi-offense, so that conviction or acquittal for one consequence bars prosecution for the others under double jeopardy
hints: Imprudence is the crime itself, not a mode of committing it.
The consequences only determine the penalty.
why: RPC Art. 365 punishes reckless and simple imprudence as quasi-offenses; reckless imprudence is a single crime regardless of its consequences, so prosecution for one result bars another prosecution for the other results of the same act (Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, G.R. No. 172716, November 17, 2010).
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 365; Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, G.R. No. 172716, November 17, 2010

q: Nilo's reckless driving caused a collision that killed Ola and damaged Pedro's car. He pleaded guilty to reckless imprudence resulting in slight physical injuries in one case, and was later charged with reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and damage to property for the same collision. Can the second case proceed?

alac.answer: No, the second case is barred by double jeopardy.
alac.basis: Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code punishes reckless imprudence as a quasi-offense. In Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, G.R. No. 172716, November 17, 2010, the Supreme Court held that reckless imprudence is a single crime, and its consequences on persons and property are material only in determining the penalty, so a prior conviction or acquittal for reckless imprudence bars a subsequent prosecution for the same quasi-offense regardless of its various resulting acts.
alac.application: Here, both cases arise from the same reckless act of driving that caused the collision. Nilo was already convicted of reckless imprudence for one consequence.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the second case for the other consequences of the same act must be dismissed on the ground of double jeopardy.

keyPoints: Reckless imprudence is a single quasi-offense (Art. 365)
Consequences only affect the penalty
Prior conviction bars another prosecution (Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro)
cite: Revised Penal Code, Art. 365; Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, G.R. No. 172716, November 17, 2010

q: Under RA 8484, as amended by RA 11449, which of the following is access device fraud?
choices: Paying with one's own valid credit card
Skimming, copying or counterfeiting a credit, payment or debit card and obtaining the information on it with intent to access the account
hints: RA 11449 added skimming and related acts.
Mere possession of skimming devices can also be punished.
why: RA 8484 Sec. 9, as amended by RA 11449, lists prohibited acts constituting access device fraud, including producing or using counterfeit access devices and skimming or copying payment cards to access accounts.
cite: Access Devices Regulation Act (RA 8484, as amended by RA 11449), Sec. 9

q: A waiter secretly swiped customers' credit cards on a small device attached to his phone, then used the copied data to make online purchases. What crime did he commit?

alac.answer: He committed access device fraud under RA 8484, as amended by RA 11449.
alac.basis: Section 9 of RA 8484, as amended by RA 11449, declares unlawful as access device fraud, among others, producing, using or trafficking in counterfeit access devices, and skimming, copying or counterfeiting any credit card, payment card or debit card, and obtaining any information therein with the intent of accessing the account and operating the same.
alac.application: Here, the waiter used a device to copy the card data (skimming) and then used the data to make purchases, which is using a counterfeit access device to access the customers' accounts.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable for access device fraud under RA 8484, as amended (aside from possible cybercrime liability).

keyPoints: Access device fraud (RA 8484, Sec. 9, as amended by RA 11449)
Skimming and copying cards
Use of the copied data to access accounts
cite: Access Devices Regulation Act (RA 8484, as amended by RA 11449), Sec. 9

q: Under RA 10883, carnapping is:
choices: Borrowing a car with the owner's consent
The taking, with intent to gain, of a motor vehicle belonging to another without consent, or by violence, intimidation or force upon things
hints: The value of the vehicle does not affect the basic penalty.
If the driver is killed, the penalty is life imprisonment.
why: RA 10883 Sec. 3: carnapping is the taking with intent to gain of another's motor vehicle without consent or by violence, intimidation or force upon things; penalties apply regardless of the vehicle's value, and are higher when the owner, driver or occupant is killed or raped.
cite: New Anti-Carnapping Act of 2016 (RA 10883), Secs. 3-4

q: Rico asked to test-drive a car being sold by its owner, then drove away and never returned it, later selling it. He argues that he committed only estafa because the owner voluntarily gave him the keys. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Rico committed carnapping.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 10883 defines carnapping as the taking, with intent to gain, of a motor vehicle belonging to another without the latter's consent, or by means of violence against or intimidation of persons, or by using force upon things. The owner's consent to a limited, temporary use, such as a test drive, is not consent to the taking of the vehicle itself.
alac.application: Here, the owner allowed Rico only to test-drive the car. Rico drove it away permanently and sold it, with intent to gain and without the owner's consent to such taking.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rico is liable for carnapping under RA 10883, punished regardless of the car's value.

keyPoints: Carnapping defined (RA 10883, Sec. 3)
Consent to a test drive is not consent to the taking
Penalty regardless of value
cite: New Anti-Carnapping Act of 2016 (RA 10883), Secs. 3-4

q: Under Section 5 of PD 1612, mere possession of any article which has been the subject of robbery or theft is:
hints: The fence need not have participated in the robbery or theft.
Fencing is a separate crime from the theft.
why: PD 1612 Sec. 2: fencing is buying, receiving, possessing, selling or dealing in anything of value which one knows, or should know, to have been derived from robbery or theft; Sec. 5: mere possession of stolen goods is prima facie evidence of fencing (Dizon-Pamintuan v. People, G.R. No. 111426, July 11, 1994).
cite: Anti-Fencing Law (PD 1612), Secs. 2 and 5; Dizon-Pamintuan v. People, G.R. No. 111426, July 11, 1994

q: A jewelry shop owner bought diamond rings at one-fifth of their value from a stranger who had no receipts. The rings turned out to have been stolen. The owner says he did not know they were stolen. Is he liable for fencing?

alac.answer: Yes, he may be held liable for fencing.
alac.basis: Section 2 of PD 1612 defines fencing as the act of any person who, with intent to gain, shall buy, receive, possess, or deal in any article which he knows, or should be known to him, to have been derived from the proceeds of robbery or theft. Section 5 provides that mere possession of any article which has been the subject of robbery or thievery shall be prima facie evidence of fencing. In Dizon-Pamintuan v. People, G.R. No. 111426, July 11, 1994, the Supreme Court held that knowledge may be inferred from circumstances such as a very low price.
alac.application: Here, the owner possessed stolen rings, giving rise to the presumption. He bought them at one-fifth of their value from a stranger without receipts, circumstances that should have alerted a jewelry dealer that the rings were stolen.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the owner is liable for fencing unless he rebuts the presumption with credible evidence of good faith.

keyPoints: Fencing defined (PD 1612, Sec. 2)
Possession of stolen goods is prima facie evidence (Sec. 5)
Knowledge inferred from circumstances (Dizon-Pamintuan v. People)
cite: Anti-Fencing Law (PD 1612), Secs. 2 and 5; Dizon-Pamintuan v. People, G.R. No. 111426, July 11, 1994

q: Under RA 12010, a person who sells or lends his financial account to be used for receiving proceeds known to come from crimes or social engineering schemes is a:
hints: Banks and e-wallets are covered.
The law targets accounts used to move scam proceeds.
why: RA 12010 Sec. 4 punishes money muling: using, opening under a fictitious name, buying, selling or lending a financial account, or recruiting others to do so, to receive or transfer proceeds known to be derived from crimes or social engineering schemes; Sec. 5 punishes social engineering schemes and economic sabotage.
cite: Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act (RA 12010), Sec. 4

q: Sam lent his e-wallet account to a stranger for P2,000, knowing it would be used to receive money from people tricked by fake online job offers. Is Sam liable under RA 12010?

alac.answer: Yes, Sam is liable as a money mule.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 12010 provides that a person performing any of the listed acts, such as selling or lending a financial account, for the purpose of obtaining, receiving, depositing, transferring, or withdrawing proceeds that are known to be derived from crimes, offenses, or social engineering schemes, shall be considered as a money mule.
alac.application: Here, Sam lent his e-wallet account, a financial account, for a fee, knowing it would be used to receive proceeds of a fake job scam, a social engineering scheme.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sam is liable for money muling under RA 12010.

keyPoints: Money muling (RA 12010, Sec. 4)
Selling or lending a financial account
Knowledge that proceeds come from crimes or scams
cite: Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act (RA 12010), Sec. 4

q: Under Section 3(e) of RA 3019, a public officer commits a corrupt practice by causing undue injury to any party or giving unwarranted benefits through:
choices: Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence
hints: The three modes are alternative.
Sec. 3(b) punishes requesting or receiving gifts in government contracts.
why: RA 3019 Sec. 3(e): causing undue injury to any party, including the Government, or giving unwarranted benefits to a private party, in the discharge of official functions, through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence; it may be committed through either mode.
cite: Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended), Sec. 3(e)

q: A mayor awarded a P20 million road contract, without public bidding, to a company owned by his brother-in-law, which had no track record; the road was never finished. What crime did the mayor commit?

alac.answer: The mayor violated Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
alac.basis: Section 3(e) of RA 3019 declares as a corrupt practice causing any undue injury to any party, including the Government, or giving any private party any unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference in the discharge of official functions through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence.
alac.application: Here, the mayor, in the discharge of his functions, awarded the contract without bidding to his brother-in-law's unqualified company, showing manifest partiality. The company received an unwarranted benefit, and the government suffered undue injury because the road was not finished.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the mayor is liable under Section 3(e) of RA 3019 (aside from possible violations of procurement laws).

keyPoints: Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019
Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence
Undue injury or unwarranted benefit
cite: Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended), Sec. 3(e)

q: Under the Anti-Hazing Act, as amended by RA 11053, the presence of a person during a hazing is:
choices: Prima facie evidence of participation as a principal, unless he prevented it or promptly reported it
hints: The victim's consent is not a defense.
Hazing is malum prohibitum.
why: RA 11053 defines hazing as acts causing physical or psychological suffering in initiation rites for admission or continued membership; it prohibits all hazing, and the presence of a person during the hazing is prima facie evidence of participation as principal unless he prevented it or promptly reported it. Hazing is malum prohibitum (Dungo v. People, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015).
cite: Anti-Hazing Act (RA 8049, as amended by RA 11053); Dungo v. People, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015

q: During a fraternity initiation, members paddled a neophyte, who died. Tom, a member, was present but only watched and did not report the incident. He argues that he did not touch the neophyte, and that the neophyte consented. Is Tom liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Tom may be held liable as a principal.
alac.basis: RA 8049, as amended by RA 11053, defines hazing as any act that results in physical or psychological suffering inflicted on a recruit as part of an initiation rite. It provides that the presence of any person, even if not a member, during the hazing is prima facie evidence of participation therein as a principal unless such person prevented the commission of the acts or promptly reported them to the authorities. In Dungo v. People, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015, the Supreme Court held that hazing is malum prohibitum, so the victim's consent and lack of criminal intent are not defenses.
alac.application: Here, Tom was present during the paddling and neither prevented it nor reported it. The neophyte's consent does not excuse the hazing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tom is presumed to have participated as a principal and may be convicted unless he rebuts the presumption.

keyPoints: Hazing defined (RA 11053)
Presence is prima facie evidence of participation
Malum prohibitum; consent no defense (Dungo v. People)
cite: Anti-Hazing Act (RA 8049, as amended by RA 11053); Dungo v. People, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015

q: Under BP 702, as amended by RA 10932, a hospital may NOT:
choices: Demand a deposit or advance payment as a prerequisite for administering basic emergency care
Refer a stable patient to another hospital
hints: The law covers public and private hospitals.
Liability extends to officers and the hospital.
why: BP 702, as amended by RA 10932, prohibits hospitals and clinics from requesting deposits or advance payments as a prerequisite for basic emergency care, confinement or treatment in emergency or serious cases, and from refusing such care; responsible officers and the hospital are penalized.
cite: Anti-Hospital Deposit Law (BP 702, as amended by RA 10932)

q: A gunshot victim was brought to a private hospital's emergency room. The cashier refused to admit him until his family paid a P20,000 deposit. The victim died while waiting. Who is liable?

alac.answer: The hospital's responsible officers and employees, and the hospital itself, are liable under BP 702, as amended by RA 10932.
alac.basis: BP 702, as amended by RA 10932, makes it unlawful for any proprietor, president, director, manager or any other officer or medical practitioner or employee of a hospital or medical clinic to request, solicit, demand or accept any deposit or any other form of advance payment as a prerequisite for administering basic emergency care to any patient, or to refuse to administer medical treatment and support in emergency cases. Higher penalties apply when the refusal results in death.
alac.application: Here, the gunshot victim was an emergency case. The hospital, through its cashier, demanded a deposit before admission, and the victim died for lack of care.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the responsible officers and employees are criminally liable, and the hospital may also be penalized, with heavier penalties because death resulted.

keyPoints: No deposit for basic emergency care (BP 702, as amended by RA 10932)
Liability of officers, employees and the hospital
Heavier penalty when death results
cite: Anti-Hospital Deposit Law (BP 702, as amended by RA 10932)

q: Money laundering under Section 4 of RA 9160, as amended, is committed by one who, knowing that property represents proceeds of an unlawful activity:
choices: Transacts, converts, transfers, conceals or disguises it, or facilitates the offense
hints: The predicate offenses are listed in Sec. 3(i).
It is a separate crime from the predicate offense.
why: RA 9160 Sec. 4: money laundering is transacting proceeds of an unlawful activity to make them appear legitimate; it is separate from the predicate offense, and a prior conviction for the unlawful activity is not required.
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended), Sec. 4

q: Ursula, knowing her husband earned P30 million from kidnapping for ransom, deposited it in several bank accounts in her name and used it to buy shares of stock. She claims she did not take part in the kidnapping. Is she liable for money laundering?

alac.answer: Yes, Ursula is liable for money laundering.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 9160, as amended, provides that money laundering is a crime whereby the proceeds of an unlawful activity are transacted, thereby making them appear to have originated from legitimate sources, committed by any person who, knowing that any monetary instrument or property represents the proceeds of any unlawful activity, transacts it, or converts, transfers, conceals or disguises it. Kidnapping for ransom is an unlawful activity under Section 3(i).
alac.application: Here, Ursula knew the money came from kidnapping for ransom, and she deposited it in her own accounts and converted it into shares of stock, disguising its origin. Her non-participation in the kidnapping does not matter, since money laundering is a separate crime.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ursula is liable for money laundering.

keyPoints: Money laundering defined (RA 9160, Sec. 4)
Knowledge of the illegal source
Separate from the predicate offense
cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160, as amended), Sec. 4

q: Under RA 11930, online sexual abuse or exploitation of children (OSAEC) refers to:
choices: The use of ICT as a means to abuse and/or exploit children sexually, including offline abuse combined with an online component
hints: Mere possession of CSAEM is punished.
Parents or guardians who facilitate are severely punished.
why: RA 11930 defines OSAEC and CSAEM (child sexual abuse or exploitation material) and penalizes producing, distributing, possessing, streaming and facilitating them, and imposes duties on internet intermediaries, banks and others.
cite: Anti-OSAEC and Anti-CSAEM Act (RA 11930), Secs. 3-4

q: A mother livestreamed her 10-year-old daughter performing sexual acts for foreign viewers who paid her online. What crime did she commit?

alac.answer: She committed online sexual abuse or exploitation of children under RA 11930.
alac.basis: RA 11930 defines online sexual abuse or exploitation of children as the use of ICT as a means to abuse and/or exploit children sexually, including cases in which offline child abuse is combined with an online component, and penalizes, among others, the production and live-streaming of child sexual abuse or exploitation material, with heavier penalties when the offender is a parent or guardian.
alac.application: Here, the mother used ICT, livestreaming, to sexually exploit her daughter for payment. As the child's parent, she is subject to the higher penalty.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the mother is liable for OSAEC under RA 11930, aside from liability under RA 7610 and the anti-trafficking law.

keyPoints: OSAEC defined (RA 11930)
Live-streaming of child sexual abuse
Heavier penalty for parents or guardians
cite: Anti-OSAEC and Anti-CSAEM Act (RA 11930), Secs. 3-4

q: Under RA 9995, copying, selling or showing a private sexual video is punishable:
choices: Only if the video was taken without consent
Even if the person consented to the recording, if there was no consent to its distribution
hints: Consent to record is not consent to share.
Online posting is covered.
why: RA 9995 punishes taking photos or videos of sexual acts or private areas without consent under circumstances of reasonable expectation of privacy, and copying, reproducing, selling, distributing or showing them, notwithstanding consent to the recording.
cite: Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act (RA 9995), Secs. 3-4

q: Victor and his girlfriend agreed to record their intimate moments on his phone. After their breakup, he sent the video to his friends. Is he liable under RA 9995?

alac.answer: Yes, Victor is liable under RA 9995.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 9995 prohibits, among others, copying, reproducing, selling, distributing, publishing or broadcasting a photo or video of a sexual act or private area of a person, and showing or exhibiting it, whether in print or broadcast media or online, without the written consent of the person depicted. The law provides that the prohibition applies notwithstanding that consent to record or take photo or video coverage was given.
alac.application: Here, the girlfriend consented only to the recording, not to the video being shared. Victor sent it to his friends without her consent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Victor is liable for photo and video voyeurism (and possibly psychological violence under RA 9262).

keyPoints: Prohibited acts under RA 9995
Consent to record is not consent to distribute
Online distribution covered
cite: Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act (RA 9995), Secs. 3-4

q: According to People v. Puno, PD 532 on highway robbery applies to:
choices: Any robbery that happens to occur on a road
Robbery committed indiscriminately against any person on Philippine highways, by persons organized for that purpose
hints: The purpose is to deter brigandage, not every robbery on a road.
Isolated robberies remain under the RPC.
why: PD 532 Sec. 2 defines highway robbery/brigandage; People v. Puno, G.R. No. 97471, February 17, 1993, held that it punishes robbery committed indiscriminately against any person on highways (as brigands), not an isolated robbery of a specific victim that happens to be on a highway, which is robbery under the RPC.
cite: Anti-Piracy and Anti-Highway Robbery Law (PD 532), Sec. 2; People v. Puno, G.R. No. 97471, February 17, 1993

q: Two men who held up a specific businessman in his car on a highway because they knew he carried cash were charged with highway robbery under PD 532. Is the charge correct?

alac.answer: No; the crime is robbery under the Revised Penal Code, not highway robbery under PD 532.
alac.basis: Section 2 of PD 532 defines highway robbery as the taking away of the property of another by means of violence or intimidation committed by any person on any Philippine highway. In People v. Puno, G.R. No. 97471, February 17, 1993, the Supreme Court held that PD 532 punishes robbery committed indiscriminately against persons on highways by groups organized for that purpose, and not acts of robbery committed against a predetermined or particular victim, which are punished under the Revised Penal Code.
alac.application: Here, the men targeted a specific businessman because they knew he carried cash. The robbery was against a particular victim, not an indiscriminate attack on highway travelers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they should be charged with robbery under the Revised Penal Code.

keyPoints: Highway robbery defined (PD 532, Sec. 2)
Indiscriminate robbery on highways (People v. Puno)
Robbery of a particular victim is under the RPC
cite: Anti-Piracy and Anti-Highway Robbery Law (PD 532), Sec. 2; People v. Puno, G.R. No. 97471, February 17, 1993

q: Plunder under RA 7080, as amended, is committed by a public officer who amasses ill-gotten wealth:
choices: Through a single act of bribery of any amount
Through a combination or series of overt or criminal acts in the aggregate amount of at least P50 million
hints: 'Combination' means at least two acts of different categories; 'series' means two or more acts of the same category.
The threshold was lowered from P75 million to P50 million.
why: RA 7080 Sec. 2, as amended by RA 7659: plunder is the amassing of ill-gotten wealth of at least P50 million through a combination or series of overt or criminal acts listed in Sec. 1(d); co-conspirators who are private persons are also liable; the law was upheld in Estrada v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 148560, November 19, 2001.
cite: Anti-Plunder Act (RA 7080, as amended by RA 7659), Secs. 1-2

q: A governor received kickbacks from three road contractors over two years, totaling P60 million, and deposited them in accounts under dummies' names. What crime did he commit?

alac.answer: The governor committed plunder.
alac.basis: Section 2 of RA 7080, as amended by RA 7659, punishes any public officer who, by himself or in connivance with others, amasses, accumulates or acquires ill-gotten wealth through a combination or series of overt or criminal acts described in Section 1(d), in the aggregate amount of at least P50 million. Section 1(d) includes receiving any commission, kickback or other pecuniary benefit in connection with any government contract. In Estrada v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 148560, November 19, 2001, the Supreme Court upheld the law.
alac.application: Here, the governor received kickbacks from three contractors, a series of overt acts of the same kind, totaling P60 million, above the P50 million threshold.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the governor is liable for plunder, and the dummies may be liable as co-conspirators.

keyPoints: Plunder (RA 7080, Sec. 2, as amended)
Combination or series of overt acts
Aggregate of at least P50 million
cite: Anti-Plunder Act (RA 7080, as amended by RA 7659), Secs. 1-2

q: Under RA 7877, sexual harassment in a work, education or training environment requires that the offender:
choices: Has authority, influence or moral ascendancy over the victim and demands, requests or requires a sexual favor
hints: The demand may be implied from conduct.
Acceptance of the demand is not required.
why: RA 7877 Sec. 3: sexual harassment is committed by one with authority, influence or moral ascendancy who demands, requests or requires a sexual favor, regardless of whether it is accepted; the demand need not be explicit (Domingo v. Rayala, G.R. No. 155831, February 18, 2008). The Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313) covers peer and public-space harassment.
cite: Anti-Sexual Harassment Act (RA 7877), Sec. 3; Domingo v. Rayala, G.R. No. 155831, February 18, 2008

q: A department head repeatedly held his subordinate's hand, kissed her cheek, and told her that her promotion would be "easier" if she were "nice" to him. He never expressly asked for sex. Is this sexual harassment under RA 7877?

alac.answer: Yes, this is sexual harassment under RA 7877.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 7877 provides that work-related sexual harassment is committed by an employer, manager, supervisor or any other person who, having authority, influence or moral ascendancy over another in a work environment, demands, requests or otherwise requires any sexual favor from the other, regardless of whether the demand is accepted, including when the favor is made a condition for promotion. In Domingo v. Rayala, G.R. No. 155831, February 18, 2008, the Supreme Court held that the demand for a sexual favor need not be express; it may be inferred from the acts of the offender.
alac.application: Here, the department head had authority over the subordinate. His physical advances and his statement linking her promotion to her being "nice" to him show an implied demand for a sexual favor as a condition for promotion.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he committed sexual harassment under RA 7877.

keyPoints: Work-related sexual harassment (RA 7877, Sec. 3)
Authority, influence or moral ascendancy
Implied demand suffices (Domingo v. Rayala)
cite: Anti-Sexual Harassment Act (RA 7877), Sec. 3; Domingo v. Rayala, G.R. No. 155831, February 18, 2008

q: In Calleja v. Executive Secretary, the Supreme Court:
choices: Struck down the entire Anti-Terrorism Act
Upheld most of the Anti-Terrorism Act but struck down the qualifier in the proviso of Sec. 4 on advocacy, protest and dissent, and a mode of designation in Sec. 25
Held that terrorism is not a crime
hints: Purpose is an element.
Legitimate dissent is excluded.
why: RA 11479 Sec. 4 defines terrorism by the acts listed and their purpose (to intimidate the public, coerce the government, or destabilize fundamental structures); advocacy, protest and dissent are not terrorism if not intended to cause death or serious harm. Calleja v. Executive Secretary, G.R. No. 252578, December 7, 2021, upheld most of the law but struck down parts of Sec. 4's proviso and Sec. 25.
cite: Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 (RA 11479), Sec. 4; Calleja v. Executive Secretary, G.R. No. 252578, December 7, 2021

q: During a peaceful rally against a new tax, organizers blocked a road for an hour, causing traffic. The police charged them with terrorism under RA 11479. Will the charge prosper?

alac.answer: No, the charge will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 11479 defines terrorism as committed by any person who engages in acts intended to cause death or serious bodily injury, extensive damage to public or private property, or similar acts, when the purpose is to intimidate the public, create an atmosphere of fear, or seriously destabilize fundamental structures. The proviso excludes advocacy, protest, dissent, stoppage of work and similar exercises of civil and political rights that are not intended to cause death or serious physical harm, to endanger a person's life, or to create a serious risk to public safety. In Calleja v. Executive Secretary, G.R. No. 252578, December 7, 2021, the Supreme Court upheld this exclusion while striking down a qualifier that made it too narrow.
alac.application: Here, the organizers held a peaceful rally and briefly blocked a road, without any intent to cause death, serious injury, or serious risk to public safety. This is protected protest and dissent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the terrorism charge must be dismissed, although the organizers may face liability for any permit or traffic violations.

keyPoints: Terrorism defined (RA 11479, Sec. 4)
Exclusion for advocacy, protest and dissent
Calleja v. Executive Secretary
cite: Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 (RA 11479), Sec. 4; Calleja v. Executive Secretary, G.R. No. 252578, December 7, 2021

q: Under RA 9745, torture is committed by:
choices: Any private person who hurts another
A person in authority or agent, or with his consent or acquiescence, who intentionally inflicts severe physical or mental pain on a person for purposes such as obtaining information or a confession
A parent who disciplines a child
hints: Torture cannot be justified by war or emergency.
Confessions obtained by torture are inadmissible.
why: RA 9745 Sec. 3 defines torture by a person in authority or agent (or at their instigation or with their acquiescence) intentionally inflicting severe pain or suffering for purposes such as extracting a confession, punishment or intimidation; it is a separate crime, not absorbed by other crimes, and no exceptional circumstance justifies it.
cite: Anti-Torture Act of 2009 (RA 9745), Sec. 3

q: Police officers repeatedly suffocated a robbery suspect with a plastic bag to force him to confess. He confessed. What is their liability, and is the confession admissible?

alac.answer: The officers are liable for torture under RA 9745, and the confession is inadmissible.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 9745 defines torture as an act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, when inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a person in authority or agent. The Act declares inadmissible any confession or statement obtained as a result of torture.
alac.application: Here, the police officers, who are agents of persons in authority, suffocated the suspect, which inflicted severe pain, in order to obtain a confession.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the officers are liable for torture, which is a separate crime, and the confession cannot be used as evidence against the suspect.

keyPoints: Torture defined (RA 9745, Sec. 3)
Infliction of severe pain by persons in authority or agents to obtain a confession
Confession inadmissible
cite: Anti-Torture Act of 2009 (RA 9745), Sec. 3

q: Under RA 9208, as amended, in the trafficking of a child for sexual exploitation:
choices: The child's consent is a defense
The child's consent is immaterial, and the use of force, fraud or coercion need not be proved
hints: Entrapment does not negate trafficking.
Qualified trafficking applies when the victim is a child.
why: RA 9208, as amended by RA 10364: trafficking is the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harboring or receipt of persons, with or without consent, by means of force, fraud, deception, abuse of vulnerability, or payments, for exploitation; when the victim is a child, the means need not be proved, and consent is immaterial (People v. Casio, G.R. No. 211465, December 3, 2014).
cite: Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act (RA 9208, as amended by RA 10364), Secs. 3-4; People v. Casio, G.R. No. 211465, December 3, 2014

q: In a police entrapment operation, Casey offered two 16-year-old girls to an undercover officer for sex in exchange for money. The girls said they agreed to it. Casey argues that the girls consented and that no one was actually exploited. Is she liable for trafficking?

alac.answer: Yes, Casey is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.
alac.basis: RA 9208, as amended by RA 10364, defines trafficking in persons as the recruitment, transportation, transfer or harboring, or receipt of persons with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for the purpose of exploitation, including prostitution; trafficking is qualified when the victim is a child. In People v. Casio, G.R. No. 211465, December 3, 2014, the Supreme Court held that the victim's consent is immaterial, that when the victim is a child the means employed need not be proved, and that the crime is consummated even in an entrapment operation.
alac.application: Here, Casey recruited and offered two minors for sex in exchange for money, for the purpose of prostitution. Their consent does not matter, and the entrapment does not negate the crime.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Casey is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.

keyPoints: Trafficking defined (RA 9208, as amended)
Consent of the victim immaterial
Children: means need not be proved; entrapment does not negate (People v. Casio)
cite: Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act (RA 9208, as amended by RA 10364), Secs. 3-4; People v. Casio, G.R. No. 211465, December 3, 2014

q: Under Section 26 of RA 9262, a woman found to suffer from battered woman syndrome who kills or injures her abuser:
choices: Incurs no criminal and civil liability, even if the requisites of self-defense are absent
hints: A dating relationship is enough.
Economic abuse, such as withholding support, is covered.
why: RA 9262 Sec. 3 defines violence against women and children by a husband, former husband, or partner in a sexual or dating relationship or with a common child, including physical, sexual, psychological and economic abuse; Sec. 26: battered woman syndrome is a justifying circumstance even without the elements of self-defense (cf. People v. Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004).
cite: Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act (RA 9262), Secs. 3, 5 and 26; People v. Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004

q: After years of beatings, Lani, diagnosed by experts with battered woman syndrome, stabbed her sleeping husband to death after he threatened to kill her the next morning. Is she criminally liable?

alac.answer: No, Lani incurs no criminal or civil liability under Section 26 of RA 9262.
alac.basis: Section 26 of RA 9262 provides that victim-survivors who are found by the courts to be suffering from battered woman syndrome do not incur any criminal and civil liability notwithstanding the absence of any of the elements for justifying circumstances of self-defense under the Revised Penal Code. RA 9262 covers violence committed by any person against a woman who is his wife.
alac.application: Here, Lani was repeatedly beaten by her husband and was found by experts to suffer from battered woman syndrome. Although the husband was asleep, so there was no actual unlawful aggression at that moment, Section 26 does not require the elements of self-defense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, if the court finds that she suffers from battered woman syndrome, Lani is exempt from criminal and civil liability.

keyPoints: VAWC covers violence against wives and partners (RA 9262, Sec. 3)
Battered woman syndrome as a defense (Sec. 26)
No need for the elements of self-defense
cite: Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act (RA 9262), Secs. 3, 5 and 26; People v. Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004

q: Under RA 4200, as interpreted in Ramirez v. Court of Appeals, secretly recording a private conversation is unlawful:
choices: Only if done by a third person
Even if done by a party to the conversation, without the authorization of all the parties
hints: Consent of all parties is required.
Recordings obtained in violation are inadmissible.
why: RA 4200 Sec. 1 prohibits secretly overhearing, intercepting or recording a private communication without authorization of all parties; a party to the conversation who secretly records it is also liable (Ramirez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 93833, September 28, 1995); illegally obtained recordings are inadmissible.
cite: Anti-Wire Tapping Act (RA 4200), Sec. 1; Ramirez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 93833, September 28, 1995

q: In a heated private meeting, Mila secretly recorded on her phone her boss insulting her, then used the recording as evidence in a case against him. Is Mila liable under RA 4200, and is the recording admissible?

alac.answer: Yes, Mila is liable under RA 4200, and the recording is inadmissible.
alac.basis: Section 1 of RA 4200 makes it unlawful for any person, not being authorized by all the parties to any private communication or spoken word, to secretly overhear, intercept, or record such communication by using any device. In Ramirez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 93833, September 28, 1995, the Supreme Court held that the law applies even to a party to the conversation who records it secretly without the consent of the other parties. The Act also provides that recordings obtained in violation of it are inadmissible in evidence.
alac.application: Here, the meeting was private, and Mila secretly recorded it without her boss's consent. That she was a party to the conversation is no defense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mila violated RA 4200, and the recording cannot be used as evidence.

keyPoints: Prohibited secret recording (RA 4200, Sec. 1)
Applies to parties to the conversation (Ramirez v. CA)
Recording inadmissible
cite: Anti-Wire Tapping Act (RA 4200), Sec. 1; Ramirez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 93833, September 28, 1995

q: According to People v. Malngan, when a person sets fire to a house intending only to burn it, and someone dies as a result:
choices: Two crimes are committed: arson and murder
There is only one crime of arson, with death as a circumstance raising the penalty
hints: Look at the main objective of the offender.
Burning to conceal a killing: two crimes.
why: PD 1613 punishes simple arson (Sec. 1, including burning one's own property endangering others) and Art. 320 (as amended by RA 7659) destructive arson; if the main objective is to burn and death results, there is only arson; if the objective is to kill and fire is the means, it is murder; if a killing is done and fire is used to conceal it, two separate crimes (People v. Malngan, G.R. No. 170470, September 26, 2006).
cite: Arson Law (PD 1613), Sec. 1; People v. Malngan, G.R. No. 170470, September 26, 2006

q: Nora set fire to her employer's house to take revenge, intending only to destroy it. Two people inside died. What crime did she commit?

alac.answer: Nora committed arson only, with the deaths raising the penalty.
alac.basis: Section 1 of PD 1613 punishes any person who burns or sets fire to the property of another. In People v. Malngan, G.R. No. 170470, September 26, 2006, the Supreme Court held that if the main objective of the offender is the burning of the building, and death results by reason of the arson, the crime is arson only, and the resulting homicide is absorbed; if the main objective is to kill, and fire is used as the means, the crime is murder; and if the offender kills and then burns the building to conceal the killing, there are two separate crimes.
alac.application: Here, Nora's main objective was to destroy the house out of revenge; the deaths resulted from the burning.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she is liable for arson (destructive arson, if the building is of the kind covered by Art. 320), with the deaths affecting the penalty.

keyPoints: Arson (PD 1613, Sec. 1)
Main objective test (People v. Malngan)
Death resulting from arson is absorbed
cite: Arson Law (PD 1613), Sec. 1; People v. Malngan, G.R. No. 170470, September 26, 2006

q: Under BP 22, as interpreted in Dico v. Court of Appeals, the prima facie presumption of knowledge of insufficient funds arises only if:
choices: The drawer received a written notice of dishonor and failed to pay or make arrangements within five banking days
hints: Notice of dishonor must be in writing and received.
Payment within five banking days is a defense.
why: BP 22 Sec. 1 punishes issuing a check knowing of insufficient funds, which is later dishonored; Sec. 2: dishonor upon presentment within 90 days is prima facie evidence of knowledge unless the drawer pays within five banking days after receiving notice of dishonor. Receipt of a written notice must be proved (Dico v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 141669, February 28, 2005). AC 12-2000 and 13-2001 allow a fine as the preferred penalty in proper cases.
cite: Bouncing Checks Law (BP 22), Secs. 1-2; Dico v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 141669, February 28, 2005

q: Omar's check was dishonored for insufficient funds. The payee only called Omar by phone to inform him, and then filed a BP 22 case. Omar paid in full ten days after the call. Should Omar be convicted?

alac.answer: No, Omar should be acquitted.
alac.basis: Section 1 of BP 22 requires that the drawer knew at the time of issue that he did not have sufficient funds. Section 2 provides that dishonor of a check presented within ninety days shall be prima facie evidence of such knowledge unless the drawer pays the holder within five banking days after receiving notice that the check has not been paid. In Dico v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 141669, February 28, 2005, the Supreme Court held that the notice of dishonor must be in writing and actually received by the drawer, and that without it, the presumption of knowledge does not arise.
alac.application: Here, Omar received only a phone call, not a written notice of dishonor. The presumption of knowledge does not arise, and the prosecution offered no other proof of his knowledge at the time of issue.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Omar must be acquitted, though he remains liable for any unpaid civil obligation.

keyPoints: Elements of BP 22 (Sec. 1)
Presumption of knowledge requires written notice of dishonor (Sec. 2)
Dico v. Court of Appeals
cite: Bouncing Checks Law (BP 22), Secs. 1-2; Dico v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 141669, February 28, 2005

q: Under RA 6713, public officials and employees are required to:
choices: File under oath a statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN), including those of their spouses and unmarried children under 18 living in their households
hints: The public has the right to know the SALN.
Gifts in the course of official duties are prohibited.
why: RA 6713 Sec. 7 prohibits financial and material interest in transactions requiring their approval, outside employment, disclosure of confidential information, and soliciting or accepting gifts in connection with official duties; Sec. 8 requires the sworn SALN and disclosure of business interests.
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees (RA 6713), Secs. 7-8

q: A BIR examiner, while auditing a company, accepted a free week-long vacation abroad from the company's owner, "as a gift among friends." Did the examiner violate RA 6713?

alac.answer: Yes, the examiner violated RA 6713.
alac.basis: Section 7(d) of RA 6713 prohibits public officials and employees from soliciting or accepting, directly or indirectly, any gift, gratuity, favor, entertainment, loan or anything of monetary value from any person in the course of their official duties or in connection with any operation being regulated by, or any transaction which may be affected by the functions of their office.
alac.application: Here, the examiner accepted a valuable vacation from the owner of the company he was auditing, a transaction directly affected by the functions of his office. Calling it a gift among friends does not take it out of the prohibition.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the examiner violated Section 7(d) of RA 6713 and may be prosecuted and disciplined (aside from possible liability under RA 3019).

keyPoints: Prohibited acts (RA 6713, Sec. 7)
No gifts in connection with official duties
SALN requirement (Sec. 8)
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees (RA 6713), Secs. 7-8

q: Under Section 29 of RA 10591, when a loose firearm is used in committing homicide:
choices: The accused is liable for two separate crimes
The use of the loose firearm is considered an aggravating circumstance of the homicide
The firearm offense absorbs the homicide
hints: A 'loose firearm' is unregistered or unlicensed.
If no other crime is committed, illegal possession is punished separately.
why: RA 10591 Sec. 28 punishes unlawful acquisition or possession of firearms and ammunition; Sec. 29: use of a loose firearm inherent in a crime is aggravating; if the crime has a penalty lower than illegal possession, the penalty for illegal possession is imposed; if the crime is rebellion, insurrection, sedition or coup, it is absorbed.
cite: Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act (RA 10591), Secs. 28-29

q: Pat shot and killed a man with an unlicensed pistol. He was charged with homicide and, in a separate information, with illegal possession of a firearm. Should he be convicted of both?

alac.answer: No; he should be convicted only of homicide, with the use of a loose firearm as an aggravating circumstance.
alac.basis: Section 29 of RA 10591 provides that the use of a loose firearm, when inherent in the commission of a crime punishable under the Revised Penal Code or other special laws, shall be considered as an aggravating circumstance, provided that if the crime is penalized with a maximum penalty lower than that for illegal possession of firearm, the penalty for illegal possession shall be imposed in lieu of the penalty for the crime.
alac.application: Here, Pat used an unlicensed pistol to commit homicide, which carries a heavier penalty than illegal possession of a small arm. The use of the loose firearm is therefore an aggravating circumstance of the homicide, not a separate crime.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pat should be convicted only of homicide, aggravated by the use of a loose firearm, and the separate charge should be dismissed.

keyPoints: Unlawful possession (RA 10591, Sec. 28)
Use of loose firearm as aggravating (Sec. 29)
No separate conviction when used in a crime with a higher penalty
cite: Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act (RA 10591), Secs. 28-29

q: Under RA 9851, genocide requires:
choices: Killing many people for any reason
Acts such as killing or causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, religious, social or similar stable group as such
hints: The specific intent to destroy the group is essential.
RA 9851 also covers 'social' groups, wider than the Genocide Convention.
why: RA 9851 Chapter III defines war crimes, genocide (acts with intent to destroy a protected group in whole or in part, including social groups), and crimes against humanity (acts as part of a widespread or systematic attack against civilians); they do not prescribe, and superior orders are no defense.
cite: Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity (RA 9851), Ch. III

q: During a local armed conflict, a commander ordered his troops to kill all members of a particular indigenous tribe in an area so that the tribe would disappear. Under RA 9851, what crime was committed?

alac.answer: Genocide was committed, and the commander and the troops who carried out the order are liable.
alac.basis: RA 9851 punishes genocide, which includes killing members of a national, ethnic, racial, religious, social or other similar stable and permanent group, or causing them serious bodily or mental harm, with intent to destroy the group, in whole or in part, as such. The Act provides that superior orders do not relieve a person of criminal responsibility for genocide, and that commanders are responsible for crimes committed by their subordinates.
alac.application: Here, the commander ordered the killing of all members of an indigenous tribe in the area so that it would disappear, which shows the specific intent to destroy an ethnic group, in part, as such.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the commander and the troops are liable for genocide under RA 9851, and the troops cannot invoke superior orders.

keyPoints: Genocide under RA 9851
Specific intent to destroy a protected group
Superior orders no defense; command responsibility
cite: Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity (RA 9851), Ch. III

q: Under Section 4(a)(1) of RA 10175, illegal access is:
choices: The access to the whole or any part of a computer system without right
hints: 'Without right' means without authority or beyond authority.
Libel through a computer system is cyberlibel.
why: RA 10175 Ch. II lists offenses against the confidentiality, integrity and availability of computer data and systems (illegal access, illegal interception, data and system interference, misuse of devices, cyber-squatting), computer-related offenses (forgery, fraud, identity theft) and content-related offenses (cybersex, child pornography, libel). Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014, upheld most provisions.
cite: Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175), Sec. 4; Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014

q: A disgruntled IT employee, after his resignation, used his old password to log into the company's server and deleted client files. What cybercrimes did he commit?

alac.answer: He committed illegal access and data interference under RA 10175.
alac.basis: Section 4(a) of RA 10175 punishes, among others, illegal access, which is the access to the whole or any part of a computer system without right, and data interference, which is the intentional or reckless alteration, damaging, deletion or deterioration of computer data without right.
alac.application: Here, after his resignation, the employee no longer had any right to access the company's server, so his login was illegal access. Deleting client files was intentional deletion of computer data without right.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable for illegal access and data interference under RA 10175.

keyPoints: Offenses under RA 10175, Sec. 4(a)
Illegal access: access without right
Data interference: deletion of data without right
cite: Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175), Sec. 4; Disini v. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 203335, February 11, 2014

q: Under Section 38 of RA 9344, when a child under 18 at the time of the offense is found guilty:
choices: The court immediately sentences him to prison
The court, instead of pronouncing judgment of conviction, places the child under suspended sentence, without need of application
hints: Suspension of sentence is automatic.
Adults who exploit children in committing crimes are punished more severely (RA 10630).
why: RA 9344: diversion is an alternative process without formal court proceedings for children in conflict with the law; Sec. 38: automatic suspension of sentence for a child under 18 at the time of the offense found guilty, even if over 18 at the time of judgment; RA 10630 added rules on serious crimes and exploitation of children by adults.
cite: Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act (RA 9344, as amended by RA 10630), Secs. 4, 20-A and 38

q: Quin, 17 at the time he committed robbery with discernment, was found guilty when he was 19. The court sentenced him to imprisonment. Was that correct?

alac.answer: No; the court should have automatically suspended the sentence and applied the dispositions under RA 9344.
alac.basis: Section 38 of RA 9344 provides that once the child who is under eighteen years of age at the time of the commission of the offense is found guilty, the court shall determine the civil liability, but instead of pronouncing the judgment of conviction, shall place the child in conflict with the law under suspended sentence, without need of application, and the suspension applies even if the child is already eighteen or older at the time of the pronouncement of guilt. The child may then undergo rehabilitation, including in agricultural camps and training facilities.
alac.application: Here, Quin was 17 when he committed the robbery, so he was a child in conflict with the law, and since he acted with discernment he was properly tried. Though he was 19 at the time of judgment, the automatic suspension of sentence still applies.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should have suspended the sentence and committed him to the appropriate rehabilitation program, instead of imposing imprisonment outright.

keyPoints: Children in conflict with the law (RA 9344)
Automatic suspension of sentence (Sec. 38)
Applies even if over 18 at judgment
cite: Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act (RA 9344, as amended by RA 10630), Secs. 4, 20-A and 38

q: Under PD 1829, which act constitutes obstruction of justice?
choices: Preventing witnesses from testifying or from reporting a crime by bribery, misrepresentation, deceit, intimidation or force
hints: It covers acts both before and during prosecution.
Relatives harboring a suspect may still be liable under PD 1829 (unlike Art. 20 RPC).
why: PD 1829 Sec. 1 punishes anyone who knowingly or willfully obstructs or delays the apprehension of suspects and the investigation and prosecution of criminal cases by acts such as preventing witnesses from testifying, altering or destroying evidence, harboring or concealing suspects, and giving false information.
cite: Obstruction of Justice Law (PD 1829), Sec. 1

q: Ryan, a businessman, paid a witness to a murder P100,000 to leave the country so that he would not testify against Ryan's friend. What crime did Ryan commit?

alac.answer: Ryan committed obstruction of justice under PD 1829.
