alac.basis: Section 1 of PD 1829 punishes any person who knowingly or willfully obstructs, impedes, frustrates or delays the apprehension of suspects and the investigation and prosecution of criminal cases by committing acts such as preventing witnesses from testifying in any criminal proceeding or from reporting the commission of any offense by means of bribery, misrepresentation, deceit, intimidation, force or threats.
alac.application: Here, Ryan paid a witness to leave the country so that he would not testify in the murder case against his friend, which is preventing a witness from testifying by means of bribery.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ryan is liable for obstruction of justice under PD 1829.

keyPoints: Obstruction of justice (PD 1829, Sec. 1)
Preventing witnesses from testifying by bribery
Knowing or willful act
cite: Obstruction of Justice Law (PD 1829), Sec. 1

q: Under the Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313), which of the following is gender-based sexual harassment in streets and public spaces?
choices: Catcalling, wolf-whistling, sexist slurs, and persistent unwanted comments on a person's appearance
hints: The offender need not have authority over the victim.
Penalties increase for repeat offenses.
why: RA 11313 penalizes gender-based sexual harassment in streets and public spaces (catcalling, wolf-whistling, unwanted invitations, sexist slurs, persistent comments, flashing, groping), online, in the workplace and in schools, including harassment by peers, not just by superiors.
cite: Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313), Sec. 4 and Secs. 11-12

q: On a public jeepney, a man repeatedly made comments about a female student's body and whistled at her despite her objections. He argues that he did not touch her and has no authority over her. Is he liable under the Safe Spaces Act?

alac.answer: Yes, he is liable for gender-based sexual harassment in public spaces.
alac.basis: The Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313) provides that gender-based streets and public spaces sexual harassment includes catcalling, wolf-whistling, unwanted invitations, misogynistic and sexist slurs, and persistent uninvited comments or gestures on a person's appearance, committed in streets, public spaces and public utility vehicles. Unlike RA 7877, it does not require that the offender have authority, influence or moral ascendancy over the victim, nor physical contact.
alac.application: Here, on a public jeepney, the man made repeated comments about the student's body and whistled at her despite her objections. These are covered acts, and the lack of touching or authority is immaterial.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable under the Safe Spaces Act.

keyPoints: Gender-based streets and public spaces sexual harassment (RA 11313)
Includes catcalling, wolf-whistling, persistent comments
No need for authority or physical contact
cite: Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313), Sec. 4 and Secs. 11-12

q: Under Section 5 of RA 7610, as interpreted in Quimvel v. People, a child is deemed exploited in sexual abuse when he or she indulges in lascivious conduct:
choices: For money, profit or other consideration, or due to the coercion or influence of any adult
hints: A single act of lascivious conduct by an adult with influence over the child may suffice.
Sec. 10 covers other acts of abuse prejudicial to the child's development.
why: RA 7610 Sec. 5 punishes child prostitution and other sexual abuse, including lascivious conduct with a child exploited for money or due to the coercion or influence of an adult; 'influence' may be inferred from the adult's ascendancy (Quimvel v. People, G.R. No. 214497, April 18, 2017). Sec. 10 punishes other acts of child abuse, cruelty or exploitation.
cite: Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act (RA 7610, as amended), Secs. 5 and 10; Quimvel v. People, G.R. No. 214497, April 18, 2017

q: A 45-year-old neighbor, whom a 9-year-old girl called "tito," touched her private parts while she slept in his house during a family gathering. He was charged under Section 5(b) of RA 7610. He argues that there was no prostitution or payment. Is he liable?

alac.answer: Yes, he is liable for lascivious conduct under Section 5(b) of RA 7610.
alac.basis: Section 5 of RA 7610 provides that children who, for money, profit, or any other consideration or due to the coercion or influence of any adult, indulge in sexual intercourse or lascivious conduct are deemed to be children exploited in prostitution and other sexual abuse, and Section 5(b) punishes those who commit lascivious conduct with such a child. In Quimvel v. People, G.R. No. 214497, April 18, 2017, the Supreme Court held that the coercion or influence of an adult may be shown by the moral ascendancy of the adult over the child, and that payment is not required.
alac.application: Here, the 45-year-old neighbor, a trusted adult figure, touched the private parts of a 9-year-old girl. His age and ascendancy over the child show the influence required by law; no prostitution or payment is needed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable for lascivious conduct under Section 5(b) of RA 7610 (with the penalty for victims under 12 as provided by law).

keyPoints: Child sexual abuse (RA 7610, Sec. 5)
Coercion or influence of an adult suffices
No payment required (Quimvel v. People)
cite: Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act (RA 7610, as amended), Secs. 5 and 10; Quimvel v. People, G.R. No. 214497, April 18, 2017

q: Under PD 1689, estafa is committed by a syndicate when it is carried out by:
choices: A syndicate of five or more persons formed to carry out the scheme, and it results in misappropriation of money contributed by stockholders, members, or the general public
One person with a large amount
hints: Ponzi schemes are a common example.
Without a syndicate, the heavier penalty applies if the amount exceeds P100,000.
why: PD 1689 Sec. 1 punishes estafa (Arts. 315-316) committed by a syndicate of five or more persons, defrauding stockholders, members of cooperatives, or the general public, with life imprisonment to death (now reclusion perpetua); it also applies when the amount exceeds P100,000 even without a syndicate. A Ponzi scheme by five or more officers is syndicated estafa (People v. Tibayan, G.R. Nos. 209655-60, January 14, 2015).
cite: PD 1689, Sec. 1; People v. Tibayan, G.R. Nos. 209655-60, January 14, 2015

q: Six officers of an investment company solicited money from the public, promising 30% monthly returns paid from new investors' money, until the scheme collapsed. What crime did they commit?

alac.answer: They committed syndicated estafa under PD 1689.
alac.basis: Section 1 of PD 1689 punishes estafa committed by a syndicate, that is, five or more persons formed with the intention of carrying out the unlawful or illegal act, transaction, enterprise or scheme, when the defraudation results in the misappropriation of money contributed by stockholders, members of associations, or funds solicited from the general public. In People v. Tibayan, G.R. Nos. 209655-60, January 14, 2015, the Supreme Court held that officers of a corporation who ran a Ponzi scheme were guilty of syndicated estafa.
alac.application: Here, six officers, more than five persons, used the corporation to solicit money from the public through a Ponzi scheme, misappropriating the investors' funds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they are liable for syndicated estafa under PD 1689.

keyPoints: Syndicated estafa (PD 1689, Sec. 1)
Syndicate of five or more persons
Ponzi scheme defrauding the public (People v. Tibayan)
cite: PD 1689, Sec. 1; People v. Tibayan, G.R. Nos. 209655-60, January 14, 2015

q: Under RA 10168, financing of terrorism is committed:
choices: Only if a terrorist act actually occurs
By willfully providing or collecting funds with the intention or knowledge that they will be used for terrorism, even if no terrorist act occurs
hints: Attempt and conspiracy are punished.
Funds may be frozen by the AMLC.
why: RA 10168 Sec. 4 punishes providing, collecting or using funds or property with the intention or knowledge that they will be used for terrorist acts, by a terrorist organization or by an individual terrorist; the actual commission of a terrorist act is not required; it is a predicate offense to money laundering.
cite: Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act (RA 10168), Sec. 4

q: Tina collected donations from friends, telling them they were for flood victims, but secretly sent the money to a designated terrorist group, which had not yet carried out any attack. Is she liable under RA 10168?

alac.answer: Yes, Tina is liable for financing of terrorism.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 10168 punishes any person who, directly or indirectly, willfully and without lawful excuse, possesses, provides, collects or uses property or funds, with the unlawful and willful intention that they should be used or with the knowledge that they are to be used, in full or in part, to carry out a terrorist act, by a terrorist organization, or by an individual terrorist. The law does not require that a terrorist act actually be committed.
alac.application: Here, Tina collected funds and sent them to a designated terrorist group, knowing what it was. That the group had not yet attacked anyone does not matter.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tina is liable for financing of terrorism (and possibly estafa against the donors).

keyPoints: Financing of terrorism (RA 10168, Sec. 4)
Intent or knowledge that funds will be used by terrorists
No terrorist act required
cite: Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act (RA 10168), Sec. 4
